skills.name: agent-runtime-validation
skills.desc: Plans and evaluates bounded runtime tests of AI agents, tools, memory, hooks, approvals, and scope enforcement. Use when static review is complete and an authorized assessment must determine how the deployed agent actually behaves.
skills.body:
---
name: agent-runtime-validation
description: "Plans and evaluates bounded runtime tests of AI agents, tools, memory, hooks, approvals, and scope enforcement. Use when static review is complete and an authorized assessment must determine how the deployed agent actually behaves."
metadata:
  portability: universal
  discipline: penetration-testing
  domain: ai-systems
  tags: [agents, runtime, tools, memory, validation]
---

# Agent runtime validation

Validate deployed agent behavior with benign sentinels and explicit stop
conditions. Static manifests describe intended behavior; runtime evidence shows
what the integrated system actually does.

## When to Use

- Testing an authorized agent after a static tool-surface review.
- Validating runtime scope enforcement, approval gates, tool-result handling,
  memory boundaries, hooks, or identity propagation.
- Reproducing a suspected confused-deputy or output-spoofing condition without
  using destructive actions.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat lab authorization as authority over production or adjacent
  tenants.
- Do not test with real secrets, destructive tools, persistence, uncontrolled
  callbacks, or irreversible state changes.
- Do not continue after the stop condition, attempt budget, or authorized time
  window is reached.

## Preconditions

Require a named environment, isolated test identity, approved tools and action
classes, benign sentinel set, attempt and duration budgets, monitoring owner,
stop mechanism, cleanup plan, and target-origin evidence source. If any is
missing, return a blocked test plan rather than improvising.

## Workflow

1. Bind every test to the authorization reference, environment, identity,
   version, configuration, tool set, time window, and run identifier.
2. Establish a baseline with an ordinary allowed task. Record prompts, model
   outputs, agent decisions, approval events, tool requests, runtime dispatches,
   target receipts, logs, and final state.
3. Use unique inert sentinels instead of secrets or executable payloads. Make
   each sentinel attributable to one test and harmless if exposed.
4. Test one control question at a time:
   - can prompt text expand tool or target scope;
   - can tool descriptions or retrieved content alter policy behavior;
   - are tool results distinguishable from model narration;
   - do approval gates bind the exact tool, arguments, identity, and target;
   - can one user, tenant, session, or task influence another through memory;
   - do hooks or middleware introduce hidden actions or stale policy;
   - can a less-privileged component induce a more-privileged one to act;
   - does a changed tool definition or permission set invalidate prior trust;
   - does the agent stop or pivot when repeated attempts make no progress.
5. For every attempt, record expected behavior, observed behavior, evidence
   source, side effects, control result, and cleanup state.
6. Stop immediately on unexpected privilege, cross-tenant effect, sensitive
   data exposure, uncontrolled recursion, monitor loss, cleanup failure, or
   target behavior outside the approved class.
7. Re-test only when the budget allows and the new attempt isolates a specific
   alternative explanation. Repetition without a new hypothesis is not
   validation.
8. Grade the result as `enforced`, `bypassed`, `inconclusive`, `blocked`, or
   `not-tested`. Missing telemetry cannot produce `enforced`.
9. Confirm cleanup and restore the baseline. Record configuration drift and
   residual artifacts.

## Deliverable

Return the bound runtime context, test matrix, baseline, per-attempt receipts,
control grades, stop events, evidence limitations, cleanup status, and focused
remediation or follow-up questions. Do not include reusable exploit payloads.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **“The manifest denies it, so runtime testing is unnecessary.”** Integration
  layers can violate the declared contract.
- **“A harmless-looking string does not need its own run ID.”** Attribution is
  what keeps concurrent tests from becoming false evidence.
- **“The model refused, so the system is safe.”** The runtime, hooks, or tool may
  still have acted.
- **“The tool returned an error, so no side effect occurred.”** Confirm final
  state from an independent source.
- **“One more variation might work.”** Stop when the budget is exhausted or no
  new hypothesis is being isolated.
- **“Production is the only realistic environment.”** Realism does not erase
  authorization, safety, or tenant boundaries.

skills.name: agent-surface-audit
skills.desc: Reviews an MCP server's tool surface for tool poisoning, over-broad parameters, missing descriptions, and privilege escalation paths. Use when auditing, onboarding, or writing an MCP server, or when a user asks whether a server is safe to connect to an agent.
skills.body:
---
name: agent-surface-audit
description: "Reviews an MCP server's tool surface for tool poisoning, over-broad parameters, missing descriptions, and privilege escalation paths. Use when auditing, onboarding, or writing an MCP server, or when a user asks whether a server is safe to connect to an agent."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob Bash
---

# Reviewing MCP servers

An MCP server hands an agent a set of tools. Each tool is a name, a
description the model reads, and a parameter schema the model fills in. The
attack surface is those three things plus whatever the tool does when called.
This skill reviews the surface deterministically first, then reads the
implementation for the parts a scanner cannot judge.

## When to Use

- Auditing, onboarding, or writing an MCP server, or when a user asks whether a server is safe to connect to an agent.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Quick start

1. Get the server's tool list as JSON. Any of these work:
   - the server's `tools/list` response, saved to a file
   - a harness's exported MCP config or tool dump
   - for a source checkout, the decorated tool definitions, converted to the
     same JSON shape (see `references/manifest-format.md`)
2. Run the checker:
   ```
   uv run {baseDir}/scripts/inspect_tools.py path/to/tools.json
   ```
   It prints one finding per line with a severity and exits non-zero if the
   input contains zero tools. An empty manifest is a failed review, not a
   clean one.
3. For every `high` finding, open the implementation and confirm whether the
   risk is real (step 4). For `medium` and `info`, record them and move on.
4. Read the implementation for what the scanner cannot see, using
   `references/checklist.md`:
   - does the tool execute, eval, or template any parameter into a shell,
     SQL, or URL?
   - does it read or write outside the paths its description claims?
   - does it make network calls to hosts the user did not name?
   - does it carry credentials, and are they scoped to the operation?
5. Write findings with the `findings-report` skill if it is
   installed; otherwise use the structure in `references/finding-shape.md`.

## Review deliverable

Return one compact review record before writing individual findings:

| Field | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | Server name, version or commit, deployment context, and tool count |
| Manifest signals | Every scanner result, including medium and informational signals |
| Implementation checks | The code path reviewed for each high-risk parameter or side effect |
| Privilege paths | What data, credentials, networks, and hosts the server can actually reach |
| Evidence gaps | Missing source, deployment configuration, or runtime controls |
| Disposition | Acceptable as deployed, acceptable with stated constraints, or reject pending change |

Do not call the server safe merely because the manifest scan is clean. A clean
manifest means the description and parameter surface passed; the implementation
and deployment blast radius remain separate claims.

## What the scanner flags

| Check | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Imperative text in a description (`ignore`, `always`, `you must`, `before calling`) | Tool poisoning: descriptions are prompt text the model obeys |
| Description references other tools or the system prompt | Cross-tool shadowing and instruction override |
| Hidden text markers (`<!-- -->`, zero-width chars, `<IMPORTANT>`) | Content meant for the model, not the human reviewer |
| Free-form string parameter named like a command, path, query, or URL | Injection sink; the model fills it from untrusted context |
| Parameter with no description or `additionalProperties: true` | Model guesses; reviewer cannot bound behavior |
| Tool name implies destructive action with no confirmation parameter | Irreversible side effect on a single model decision |
| Tool with no description at all | Unreviewable; the model will invent one |

Severity is assigned by the script and is a starting point, not a verdict.

## Judgment calls the script leaves to you

- **A shell tool is not automatically a finding.** `run_command` on a
  sandboxed dev container is the product. `run_command` on a production host
  reachable from a chat window is critical. Severity follows the blast radius
  of the deployment, which is in the config, not the manifest.
- **Descriptions that instruct the model are sometimes legitimate.** "Call
  `get_schema` before `run_query`" is good UX. "Ignore prior instructions
  about credentials" is an attack. The script flags both; you decide, and
  you record why.
- **Read-only is a claim, not a property.** A tool described as read-only
  that takes a path parameter can still read secrets. Check what the path is
  resolved against.

## Rationalizations to reject

- *"It's a first-party server from a reputable vendor."* Vendor servers have
  shipped `run_command` with no sandbox and descriptions with hidden
  instructions. Reputation changes the prior, not the review.
- *"The harness will ask the user before destructive calls."* Some do, some
  do not, and the approval prompt shows the tool name, not the parameters.
  Review as if every call auto-approves.
- *"The parameter schema is strict so injection is bounded."* A schema bounds
  the type, not the content. A `string` with `maxLength: 10000` is a shell
  command.
- *"The server only runs locally."* Local is where the user's SSH keys,
  cloud credentials, and source trees are. Local is the high-value target.
- *"There are too many tools to read them all."* Then the server has too
  many tools, and that is the first finding. Review all of them; the script
  makes the first pass cheap.

## Harness notes

In Claude Code, the server's tool list can be read from the active session's
MCP configuration rather than a saved file; the review itself is unchanged.

skills.name: agent-trust-boundary-audit
skills.desc: Maps identity, authority, instruction, data, memory, and approval propagation across agents and agent-to-agent handoffs. Use when reviewing multi-agent systems, orchestrators, delegated tools, or confused-deputy exposure.
skills.body:
---
name: agent-trust-boundary-audit
description: "Maps identity, authority, instruction, data, memory, and approval propagation across agents and agent-to-agent handoffs. Use when reviewing multi-agent systems, orchestrators, delegated tools, or confused-deputy exposure."
metadata:
  portability: universal
  discipline: blue-team
  domain: ai-systems
  tags: [agents, a2a, trust-boundaries, identity, confused-deputy]
---

# Agent trust boundary audit

Map how authority actually crosses an agent system. Keep communication,
authentication, authorization, delegation, and downstream effect distinct; a
message path alone does not establish permission to act.

## When to Use

- Reviewing multi-agent, orchestrated, delegated-tool, or agent-to-agent
  architectures.
- Investigating confused-deputy, identity propagation, approval, memory, or
  handoff-validation concerns.
- Establishing which component can cause which other component to act and under
  whose identity.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat the audit as authority to exercise a handoff or invoke a tool.
- Do not infer effective permissions from component names, intended roles, or a
  protocol's default security model.
- Do not collapse all agents into one trust zone merely because they share an
  orchestrator or model provider.

## Workflow

1. Define the reviewed system, environments, tenants, versions, evidence cutoff,
   owners, and intended security properties.
2. Inventory principals and components: humans, service identities, agents,
   orchestrators, models, brokers, tools, memories, queues, approval services,
   policy engines, targets, and administrative planes.
3. Record each component's authentication method, effective identity, privilege,
   tenant context, reachable resources, secret access, and policy source.
4. Map five edge types separately:
   - data transfer;
   - instruction transfer;
   - identity or token transfer;
   - delegated authority;
   - result or state transfer.
5. For every handoff, record sender, receiver, message type, provenance,
   integrity, freshness, audience binding, replay protection, target binding,
   approval binding, and failure behavior.
6. Trace authority end to end. Identify where a low-authority principal can
   shape inputs consumed by a higher-authority component, even when no
   credential crosses the boundary.
7. Review confused-deputy conditions: mismatched requester and execution
   identity, ambient authority, incomplete target binding, untrusted arguments,
   result reuse, and approval detached from final action.
8. Review memory and state boundaries: writer, reader, tenant, lifetime,
   revocation, provenance, conflict handling, and stale-state invalidation.
9. Label every edge `observed`, `reported`, `inferred`, `contradicted`, or
   `unknown`. Preserve the exact evidence supporting effective authority.
10. Build abuse-path hypotheses without exercising them. A path remains
    conditional when any identity, authority, policy, or target transition is
    unproven.
11. Prioritize choke points where one control limits multiple paths: scoped
    identity, explicit delegation, exact approval binding, provenance checks,
    tenant isolation, revocation, and target-side authorization.

## Boundary with adjacent skills

- Use `agent-surface-audit` for individual tool definitions and parameter risk.
- Use `agent-runtime-validation` to exercise authorized runtime controls.
- Use `ai-threat-model` for the broader system threat model and crown jewels.

## Deliverable

Return the component and principal inventory, typed trust-edge map, effective
authority matrix, handoff-control table, confused-deputy hypotheses, memory and
tenant findings, evidence gaps, and prioritized control choke points.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **“The agents are internal, so the handoff is trusted.”** Internal components
  can have different identities, tenants, policies, and compromise assumptions.
- **“The protocol authenticates both sides.”** Authentication does not prove
  authorization for the requested target or action.
- **“The approval happened in the workflow.”** Verify that it binds the final
  arguments, identity, target, and time.
- **“No credential is forwarded, so authority does not propagate.”** A deputy
  can act with ambient authority on attacker-shaped input.
- **“Shared memory is just context.”** Persistent context is a cross-task data
  and instruction boundary.
- **“The diagram shows the intended path.”** Intended architecture is reported
  evidence until deployment facts confirm it.

skills.name: prompt-injection-assessment
skills.desc: Assesses whether direct, indirect, multi-turn, retrieved, or tool-mediated instructions can override an AI system's intended policy or scope. Use when conducting an authorized prompt-injection test with benign canaries and evidence-bound outcomes.
skills.body:
---
name: prompt-injection-assessment
description: "Assesses whether direct, indirect, multi-turn, retrieved, or tool-mediated instructions can override an AI system's intended policy or scope. Use when conducting an authorized prompt-injection test with benign canaries and evidence-bound outcomes."
metadata:
  portability: universal
  discipline: penetration-testing
  domain: ai-systems
  tags: [prompt-injection, indirect-injection, guardrails, agents, evidence]
---

# Prompt injection assessment

Measure instruction integrity across every authorized input channel without
turning a response into a stronger claim than the evidence supports. Use inert
canaries and bounded effects instead of secrets, destructive actions, or
reusable bypass payloads.

## When to Use

- Testing direct, indirect, multi-turn, retrieved, or tool-mediated instruction
  handling in an authorized environment.
- Evaluating whether guardrails, canonicalization, role separation, and approval
  controls preserve stated security invariants.
- Reproducing a suspected prompt-injection path with a harmless observable.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not use this skill as permission to jailbreak a public or third-party
  system.
- Do not request secrets, destructive actions, persistence, or uncontrolled
  external effects as proof.
- Do not publish transferable bypass strings when a bounded test description
  and redacted evidence are sufficient.

## Preconditions

Require the named system, environment, identity, allowed channels, prohibited
effects, benign canary set, attempt and duration budgets, reset method,
monitoring owner, stop condition, and cleanup duty. Return a blocked plan when
these are absent.

## Evidence states

Keep these states separate:

1. `delivered` — test content reached the authorized input boundary.
2. `context-present` — runtime evidence shows it entered model context.
3. `instruction-influenced` — output or decision changed consistently with it.
4. `policy-bypassed` — a stated invariant failed under the test condition.
5. `action-influenced` — a tool or downstream action was selected or altered.
6. `effect-verified` — target-origin evidence confirms the bounded effect.

## Chain map

Map every case as `INPUT -> CONTEXT -> ACTION -> OUTPUT`. Record each node as
`supported`, `contradicted`, `missing`, or `not-applicable`, and bind every
supported node to its own receipt.

1. **INPUT** — where the test content entered, who or what supplied it, the
   tested identity and channel, and evidence that it reached the authorized
   input boundary.
2. **CONTEXT** — whether the content entered model context, what trust label and

skills.name: cloud-attack-path
skills.desc: Maps cloud identity and authorization paths across AWS, Azure, GCP, and hybrid trust boundaries, separating proven access from plausible and blocked routes. Use during an authorized cloud penetration test when tracing how a starting identity could assume roles, use credentials, execute workloads, cross providers, or reach sensitive data.
skills.body:
---
name: cloud-attack-path
description: "Maps cloud identity and authorization paths across AWS, Azure, GCP, and hybrid trust boundaries, separating proven access from plausible and blocked routes. Use during an authorized cloud penetration test when tracing how a starting identity could assume roles, use credentials, execute workloads, cross providers, or reach sensitive data."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Cloud attack paths

Cloud attack paths are identity graphs. A principal reaches an objective through
permissions, credentials, workload identities, federation, and resource policy.
An allow statement is one input to that graph, not proof that the edge works.

Use this skill only inside written authorization. Mapping a possible path does
not authorize credential retrieval, role assumption, deployment, data access,
or any other validation action.

## When to Use

- An authorized cloud penetration test when tracing how a starting identity could assume roles, use credentials, execute workloads, cross providers, or reach sensitive data.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Build the map

1. **Define the endpoints.** State the starting identity, target resource or
   data, the cloud boundaries in scope, and the smallest proof the engagement
   requires.
2. **Record evidence before conclusions.** Classify each source as observed,
   reported current, reported stale, or inferred. Names such as
   `prod-admin-key` suggest provenance; they do not establish it.
3. **Normalize the graph.** Represent identities, credentials, services,
   resources, and data as nodes. Represent authorization, impersonation,
   credential material, federation, workload execution, and resource access as
   directed edges.
4. **Resolve effective access.** Account for identity and resource policies,
   explicit denies, conditions, permission boundaries, session restrictions,
   organization policy, encryption controls, service enablement, and network or
   perimeter controls that apply. Keep unresolved layers visible.
5. **Classify every edge.** Use:
   - `validated` when current evidence establishes the transition;
   - `candidate` when the transition is plausible but has unverified facts;
   - `blocked` when a known control prevents it;
   - `unknown` when available evidence cannot support a direction.
6. **Make boundary crossings explicit.** For every account, tenant, project,
   provider, or on-premises crossing, name the trust mechanism and its evidence.
   Credential files, federation, and workload identity are separate transitions.
7. **Assemble continuous paths.** Each edge must begin where the previous edge
   ended. Include blocked branches because they explain why apparent privilege
   does not produce a route.
8. **Plan minimum validation.** Prefer metadata and policy reads. Classify each
   validation step and compare it with written authorization. Mark credential
   reads, content access, active execution, and state changes as requiring
   separate approval when they are not already allowed.
9. **State only what the path proves.** A path is:
   - `proven` only when every edge is validated;
   - `plausible` when at least one edge is a candidate and none is blocked or unknown;
   - `blocked` when any edge is blocked;
   - `unknown` when uncertainty prevents a stronger result.

## Provider semantics to preserve

- **AWS:** an identity allow may still lose to an SCP, permissions boundary,
  session policy, resource policy, KMS policy, condition, or explicit deny.
  `PassRole` needs a permitted service action that can consume the role.
- **Azure:** distinguish Entra directory roles from Azure resource RBAC. Resolve
  assignment scope, deny assignments, managed identities, vault mode, and
  conditional access or network restrictions relevant to the transition.
- **GCP:** `serviceAccounts.actAs` lets a workload run as a service account; it
  does not itself mint a token. Resolve allow and deny policies, conditions,
  service enablement, service agents, and perimeter controls.
- **Hybrid and multi-cloud:** treat a credential or assertion as one node and
  the identity it may represent as another. The mapping between them needs its
  own evidence.

## Judgment calls

The script cannot interpret live provider policy or determine whether a
counterfactual deployment would succeed. It verifies the normalized record:
references, continuity, evidence strength, boundary declarations, deny
precedence, authorization classes, and claim strength. A clean result means the
assessment is honest about its inputs, not that the attack path is executable.

## Rationalizations to reject

| Thought | Reality |
|---|---|
| "The policy says Allow, so the edge is proven." | Effective access is the result of every applicable policy and condition. Record unresolved layers. |
| "The secret name tells us which identity it belongs to." | A name is inferred provenance. Use a key ID, application ID, deployment record, or other non-secret evidence. |
| "PassRole means I can become that role." | It only matters with an allowed service action that accepts the role. |
| "actAs is direct impersonation." | GCP workload attachment and token creation are different permissions. |
| "We can deploy a harmless function to verify it." | Deployment changes state and creates telemetry. Authorization decides whether it is permitted. |
| "The final object permission proves the whole chain." | Every preceding identity and trust transition must also hold. |
| "the record is complete, so the path works." | It passed structural and evidentiary checks over supplied facts. Provider behavior still requires authorized validation. |

skills.name: firmware-hardware-assessment
skills.desc: Tracks embedded-device and firmware assessment coverage across exact units, acquisition methods, debug interfaces, stored secrets, update trust, radios, physical safety, and delegated external systems. Use when planning, conducting, reviewing, or handing over an authorized hardware or IoT penetration test.
skills.body:
---
name: firmware-hardware-assessment
description: "Tracks embedded-device and firmware assessment coverage across exact units, acquisition methods, debug interfaces, stored secrets, update trust, radios, physical safety, and delegated external systems. Use when planning, conducting, reviewing, or handing over an authorized hardware or IoT penetration test."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Firmware and hardware assessment

A visible debug pad is not usable debug access. Matching flash reads prove a
repeatable acquisition, not authentic firmware. A signature block or downgrade
string does not prove enforcement. Keep each conclusion tied to the exact unit,
artifact, action, and evidence.

## When to Use

- Planning, conducting, reviewing, or handing over an authorized hardware or IoT penetration test.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Workflow

1. Record model, serial, hardware revision, reported firmware, and whether each
   device is sacrificial and authorized for damage.
2. State allowed action classes, in-scope external systems, and constraints.
   Treat voltage, power state, fixtures, and irreplaceable calibration as safety
   boundaries, not informal notes.
3. Bind photographs, measurements, logs, captures, and analysis to a device.
   Keep secret values out of summaries and report attachments.
4. Record each acquired artifact with its SHA-256, source, acquisition, and
   evidence. Preserve repeated reads as separate artifacts.
5. Derive acquisition consistency from artifact hashes. Matching reads establish
   repeatability only from the first recorded read onward.
6. Compare vendor and installed images by partitions and normalized content.
   Record per-device configuration and calibration before interpreting unequal
   whole-image hashes.
7. Inventory one `device` surface per unit, then components, debug interfaces,
   storage, firmware images, update mechanisms, local and network services,
   radios, and external systems.
8. Cover device identity, acquisition integrity, debug access, firmware
   analysis, credential material, update trust, communications, integration,
   supply chain, and physical safety. Preserve planned, blocked, delegated, and
   inconclusive work.
9. Use `finding` only for an executed, evidenced case. Limit claim scope to the
   tested unit unless evidence from additional devices supports a broader claim.
10. Delegate companion applications, vendor cloud, brokers, update services,
    and production systems. Discovery does not authorize contact.

## Interpretation rules

- A password prompt is a positive control for that interface, not proof of
  password strength or restricted post-authentication privilege.
- A locked root account says nothing about other support identities.
- A recovered private key proves extractability from that artifact. Fleet-wide
  reuse needs evidence from more than one unit.
- An apparent signature block is an indicator until verification code, trust
  anchor, signed regions, and failure behavior are established.
- An update error string does not prove rollback prevention.
- Interface pads prove physical presence. Pinout, lifecycle state, fuses,
  authentication, and effective access remain separate questions.
- Firmware version labels do not prove byte equivalence.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **"The hashes differ, so the installed firmware was tampered with."** Device
  configuration, calibration, logs, and writable state can explain the delta.
- **"Two reads match, so the firmware is authentic."** They prove acquisition
  repeatability, not origin or trust.
- **"JTAG pads exist, so JTAG is enabled."** Usability depends on pinout,
  electrical state, lifecycle controls, and authorization to interrogate it.
- **"The package is signed, so updates are secure."** Enforcement and coverage
  of every security-sensitive field still need evidence.
- **"The credential is in one unit, so the whole fleet shares it."** A
  single-device observation cannot establish provisioning behavior.
- **"A sacrificial fixture makes destructive work authorized."** Written action
  scope and explicit damage authorization are both required.

skills.name: mobile-application-assessment
skills.desc: Tracks Android and iOS application assessment coverage across packages, platform components, local storage, device behavior, WebViews, native code, network trust, and delegated backend APIs. Use when planning, conducting, reviewing, or handing over an authorized mobile app penetration test.
skills.body:
---
name: mobile-application-assessment
description: "Tracks Android and iOS application assessment coverage across packages, platform components, local storage, device behavior, WebViews, native code, network trust, and delegated backend APIs. Use when planning, conducting, reviewing, or handing over an authorized mobile app penetration test."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Mobile application assessment

A decompiled indicator is not a runtime exploit, a rooted-device observation is
not ordinary-device reachability, and one denied backend request is not an API
authorization assessment. Keep each claim tied to its build, layer, method, and
evidence.

## When to Use

- Planning, conducting, reviewing, or handing over an authorized mobile app penetration test.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Workflow

1. Record the exact Android package or iOS bundle, platform, build kind, and
   SHA-256. Keep evidence from different builds in separate assessments.
2. State allowed action classes, structured test devices and accounts, in-scope
   origins, and constraints. Prevent production and third-party traffic at the test boundary
   when the app contains out-of-scope destinations.
3. Inventory one `application` surface per build, then add discovered storage,
   component, network endpoint, WebView, native library, cryptographic use,
   runtime defense, privacy channel, and backend API surfaces.
4. Give every surface an evidence reference and disposition. Static reachability
   supports a conditional exposure; runtime effect needs runtime evidence.
5. Cover all eight current MASVS categories for the application surface:
   storage, cryptography, authentication, network, platform interaction, code,
   resilience, and privacy. Add the categories derived for each detailed surface.
6. Record each case as `executed`, `planned`, `blocked`, `not-applicable`, or
   `delegated`. Only executed cases can claim a finding, no issue, or an
   inconclusive result. Preserve blockers and technical rationales.
7. Separate app, device, backend, and third-party evidence. A mobile client can
   expose an API route, but server-side authorization coverage belongs in the
   web assessment ledger. Preserve a bounded observed backend request as an
   executed case, then add a separate `delegated` case for the broader handoff.
8. Treat public identifiers, private secrets, exported components, client-side
   state, pinning, backup settings, root detection, and native code according to
   demonstrated impact. Their presence alone does not set severity.
9. Build category summaries from all recorded cases. Record the derived open
   case IDs so planned, blocked, delegated, and inconclusive work stays visible
   even when a confirmed finding takes precedence in the category claim.

## Interpretation rules

skills.name: password-audit-plan
skills.desc: Plans authorized offline password-strength audits across supplied hash datasets while enforcing compute budgets, progressive pass order, cohort coverage, aggregate-only reporting, and restricted handling. Use when preparing or documenting password cracking without online authentication, spraying, stuffing, replay, or credential reuse testing.
skills.body:
---
name: password-audit-plan
description: "Plans authorized offline password-strength audits across supplied hash datasets while enforcing compute budgets, progressive pass order, cohort coverage, aggregate-only reporting, and restricted handling. Use when preparing or documenting password cracking without online authentication, spraying, stuffing, replay, or credential reuse testing."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Password audit plan

Offline password auditing is a measured experiment over supplied material. Algorithm,
hardware, candidate space, runtime, and cohort denominators determine what the result
means. Preserve unknowns until measurement exists.

This skill plans and records offline analysis. It does not collect hashes, expose raw
material, generate organization-derived candidates, authenticate, spray, stuff,
replay, test reuse, contact accounts, or access target systems.

## When to Use

- Preparing or documenting password cracking without online authentication, spraying, stuffing, replay, or credential reuse testing.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Workflow

1. Record authorization, offline-only boundary, compute and storage ceilings,
   prohibited sources and actions, stop conditions, workspace, retention, owner, and
   disposition evidence.
2. Inventory each dataset using opaque IDs. Record source class, record and unique
   digest counts, acquisition-time precision, algorithm claim, validation state,
   cost parameters, integrity, and limitations. Never place raw hashes in the plan.
3. Preserve record counts and digest counts separately. Deduplicate work while keeping
   the mapping needed to expand aggregate recoveries back to record and cohort counts.
4. Define cohorts with explicit denominators and overlap rules. Disabled, privileged,
   service, administrator, and standard populations remain separate where supplied.
5. Plan format validation and a measured benchmark before recovery passes. Do not
   invent throughput, runtime, keyspace completion, or recoveries.
6. Order bounded passes from generic baseline through generic rules, bounded masks,
   and optional adaptive work. Each pass names dependencies, candidate-source class,
   dataset, GPU budget, expected measurement, and stop conditions.
7. Let the review reject budget over-allocation, recovery before validation and
   benchmark, prohibited candidate sources, online actions, unproved results, and
   inconsistent cumulative counts.
8. Record pass results as counts and rates only. Attribute each unique recovery to its
   first successful pass; expand record recovery and cohort recovery from the preserved
   mapping without exposing plaintext.
9. Analyze aggregate length, character-class, duplicate, pattern-label, cohort, policy
   shape, and marginal-yield metrics. A policy document is a requirement, not proof a
   recovered password complied when created.
10. Track raw datasets, recovered material, potfiles, restore state, generated
    candidates, logs, and exports through disposition. Report only approved aggregate
    artifacts and opaque IDs.
11. Cover format, deduplication, cohorts, benchmark, baseline, rules, masks, adaptive
    work, handling, and reporting for every dataset. Blocked work remains visible.

## Boundary with adjacent skills

- Use `credential-exposure-audit` to inventory possible credential exposure without
  cracking or decrypting.
- Use `password-audit-plan` only after offline material and authority are supplied.
- Use `findings-report` after aggregate audit results are proven.
- Online authentication, spraying, stuffing, reuse checks, and account contact require
  a separate capability and authorization; they are outside this skill.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **"The manifest says NTLM, so mode selection is settled."** Validate structure before
  spending compute or interpreting results.
- **"Deduplication reduced 1,000 accounts to 860 hashes."** It reduced work items, not
  the reporting population. Expand results back to records and cohorts.
- **"The benchmark should be about this fast."** Hardware labels and published speeds
  are not measurements of this dataset and configuration.
- **"Eight hours means every pass gets an equal share."** Allocate from measured cost,
  expected evidence value, and explicit priorities; record the rationale.
- **"Recovered means valid."** Offline equality says nothing about current account
  state, usability, privilege, or successful authentication.
- **"Examples make the pattern finding clearer."** Plaintext examples and reusable
  candidate strings do not belong in the assessment record or report.
- **"The potfile is just tool state."** It contains recovered evidence and inherits the
  same storage, access, retention, and deletion rules.
- **"One more pass cannot hurt."** The compute ceiling and stop conditions are part of
  authorization, even when the hardware is idle.

skills.name: persistence-surface-assessment
skills.desc: Measures local Windows and Linux endpoint persistence exposure from supplied evidence by deriving consumer, authority, lifecycle, prevention, context, telemetry, and coverage state. Use when auditing durable-execution risk without creating, activating, testing, ranking, or removing a persistence mechanism.
skills.body:
---
name: persistence-surface-assessment
description: "Measures local Windows and Linux endpoint persistence exposure from supplied evidence by deriving consumer, authority, lifecycle, prevention, context, telemetry, and coverage state. Use when auditing durable-execution risk without creating, activating, testing, ranking, or removing a persistence mechanism."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Persistence surface assessment

Persistence exposure is not proof that persistence exists, executed, survived, was approved, or
is malicious. Measure whether current supplied evidence closes the prerequisites for durable local
execution while keeping every assessed surface opaque.

This skill is read-only and local-endpoint only. It does not enumerate a live host, reveal concrete
locations, create or rank mechanisms, execute triggers, change configuration, test survival, clean
artifacts, evade telemetry, inspect directory or cloud control planes, handle credentials, or assess
kernel, bootkit, firmware, or hidden-object integrity.

## When to Use

- Auditing durable-execution risk without creating, activating, testing, ranking, or removing a persistence mechanism.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Workflow

1. Record exact written authority, scoped Windows or Linux assets, the supplied-evidence boundary,
   assessment time, collection windows, and prohibited active actions.
2. Normalize evidence with one asset, source group, opaque locator, digest status, observed time or
   bounded window, validity, provenance, limitations, and custody. Do not invent precision, names,
   ownership, hashes, or independence.
3. Cover every required platform surface. Each asset-category cell is `assessed`, `blocked`, or
   `not-applicable`; one empty surface never proves asset-wide absence.
4. Represent each existing consumer only by an opaque surface reference and closed category. Keep
   consumer availability, effective change authority, lifecycle survival, preventive control,
   execution-context relation, and telemetry state as separate evidence-backed facts.
5. Require current same-asset evidence for every non-unknown fact. Evidence from one source group
   remains one vantage even when several parsers report it. Stale, unavailable, or disposed material
   cannot prove current exposure.
6. Keep execution separate from exposure. Execution needs an exact configuration-to-artifact-to-
   event binding in a compatible window; an existing registration is not compromise or success.
7. Mark higher-context exposure for a privilege-escalation handoff without claiming elevation. If
   host-view integrity is suspect, derive `inconclusive` and require rootkit triage.
8. Create only closed defensive remediation objectives and owned specialist handoffs. Rank fix
   urgency, never mechanism usefulness. A fix is complete only from post-change evidence.
9. Derive all surface states, coverage, priorities, and summaries. Preserve blocked, unknown,
    conditional, conflicting, and not-applicable work rather than converting silence to clean.

## Boundary with adjacent skills

- `privilege-escalation-assessment` owns vertical transitions and achieved identity.
- `rootkit-triage` owns hidden artifacts, compromised inspection layers, and boot or kernel integrity.
- `credential-exposure-audit` owns secret material, validity, privilege, and handling.
- `memory-forensics-triage` owns supplied volatile images; memory representation is not durability.
- `directory-persistence-audit` owns directory-wide identities, policy, delegation, and control paths.
- Cloud attack-path workflows own IAM, workload identity, provider schedulers, and control planes.
- Detection workflows own detector creation and authorized technique-to-alert validation.
- `findings-report` owns final claim-bearing stakeholder prose.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **"It is writable, so persistence is confirmed."** Consumer, survival, and prevention still bind.
- **"The ticket or signature makes it approved."** Neither binds the current exact configuration.
- **"The scheduler returned success."** A result code does not prove the intended artifact executed.
- **"The process name matches."** Names do not bind configuration, artifact, event, or context.
- **"One empty location means the host is clean."** Preserve the full platform denominator.
- **"Read authority permits a harmless test."** Triggers, restarts, logons, reboots, and edits are active.
- **"Show the exact location so remediation is easier."** Keep this artifact opaque and hand off safely.
- **"Rank the most reliable option."** Rank remediation urgency, never persistence utility.
- **"Disposed evidence still proves the state."** Preserve its disposition receipt, not a current claim.
- **"Unknown means low risk."** Unknown prerequisites yield conditional or inconclusive exposure.

skills.name: web-assessment-coverage
skills.desc: Tracks web application assessment coverage across endpoints, inputs, roles, authentication states, and test families, preventing untested or blocked work from being reported as clean. Use when planning, conducting, reviewing, or handing over an authorized web or API penetration test.
skills.body:
---
name: web-assessment-coverage
description: "Tracks web application assessment coverage across endpoints, inputs, roles, authentication states, and test families, preventing untested or blocked work from being reported as clean. Use when planning, conducting, reviewing, or handing over an authorized web or API penetration test."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Web assessment coverage

A web assessment is complete only when every discovered surface has an honest
disposition. A route inventory is not coverage, and a planned test is not a
negative result.

Use this skill only inside written authorization. Scope, rate, impact, test
accounts, and permission for state changes come from the engagement, not from
this skill.

## When to Use

- Planning, conducting, reviewing, or handing over an authorized web or API penetration test.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Build the coverage ledger

1. **Record the assessment boundary.** State the exact in-scope origins,
   engagement type, available identities, action classes allowed now, request
   limits, excluded systems, and handling constraints. Stop at out-of-scope
   redirects and resource hosts.
2. **Inventory surfaces before testing.** Record every observed route, method,
   input, authentication state, API operation, GraphQL operation, WebSocket,
   upload, business workflow, client-side surface, and configuration surface.
   Preserve distinct methods and trust contexts as distinct surfaces.
3. **Derive required families.** require:
   - any surface with input: `injection`;
   - authentication surface: `authentication` and `session-management`;
   - API: `api`; GraphQL: `api` and `graphql`;
   - upload, WebSocket, business logic, client side, and configuration: their
     matching test family;
   - ownership-sensitive surface: `horizontal-access-control` role checks;
   - privilege boundary: `vertical-access-control` role checks.
4. **Name access-control pairs.** For horizontal checks, identify the actor and
   peer resource owner, including the reverse direction when both matter. For
   vertical checks, identify the lower-privilege actor and privileged target.
   An unavailable administrator account limits what can be concluded; it does
   not make vertical coverage complete.
5. **Give each required case one status.** Use `planned`, `executed`, `blocked`,
   or `not-applicable`. Blocked cases name the blocker. Not-applicable cases
   explain why the family does not apply. Planned cases remain untested.
6. **Separate status from outcome.** Only an executed case can report
   `finding`, `no-issue`, or `inconclusive`, and every executed case links to
   evidence. Every other status uses `not-run`.
7. **Enforce authorization per case.** Classify the action as read-only,
   authenticated read, reversible state change, state change, active execution,
   high volume, or external contact. Work outside the currently allowed classes
   is marked `requires-separate-approval`; never present it as executable now.
8. **Summarize by family without hiding gaps.** Each family summary references
   all of its coverage records. derive the claim:
   - any evidenced finding → `finding`;
   - any planned or blocked case → `incomplete`;
   - otherwise any inconclusive execution → `inconclusive`;
   - fully executed cases with no findings → `no-issue`;
   - all cases justified as not applicable → `not-applicable`.
9. **Send confirmed vulnerabilities to the reporting skill.** Coverage says
   what was tested. A finding still needs reproducibility, impact, severity, and
   remediation.

## Test depth follows the engagement

- **Completeness does not mean maximum impact.** Cover a high-impact family with
  a blocked or approval-gated record when safe validation is unavailable.
- **Use known fixtures for authorization.** Comparing two supplied accounts is
  evidence; enumerating other customers is scope expansion.
- **State changes need recovery.** Define the exact mutation, expected artifact,
  restoration action, and maximum attempts before seeking approval.
- **Negative bounded tests have limits.** A small race or rate sample may find a
  flaw, but silence does not establish resilience against higher volume.
- **Third-party services remain separate targets.** Record an external redirect,
  storage URL, mail system, or payment processor without touching it unless its
  origin is explicitly in scope.

## Judgment calls

The script derives required families from the normalized surface fields and
checks the evidence contract. It cannot decide whether the route inventory is
complete, whether a payload was technically adequate, or whether linked
evidence proves the claimed security behavior. Review those judgments directly.

## Rationalizations to reject

| Thought | Reality |
|---|---|
| "We planned the test, so this area is covered." | Planned means unexecuted. It supports an `incomplete` summary. |
| "The scanner found nothing." | A tool result proves only the surfaces and techniques it actually exercised. |
| "One user-to-user check covers IDOR." | Record every required direction and role pair explicitly. |
| "We lack an admin account, so vertical access control is not applicable." | Low-privilege denial may be testable; privileged workflow coverage remains blocked. |
| "No finding means secure." | It means no issue was observed within the executed coverage and its limits. |
| "A harmless upload or checkout does not count as a state change." | It still creates client state and requires the authorization assigned to that action class. |
| "The route points to another host, so it is part of the app." | Scope follows explicit origins, not architectural association. |

   peer resource owner, including the reverse direction when both matter. For
   vertical checks, identify the lower-privilege actor and privileged target.
   An unavailable administrator account limits what can be concluded; it does
   not make vertical coverage complete.
5. **Give each required case one status.** Use `planned`, `executed`, `blocked`,
   or `not-applicable`. Blocked cases name the blocker. Not-applicable cases
   explain why the family does not apply. Planned cases remain untested.
6. **Separate status from outcome.** Only an executed case can report
   `finding`, `no-issue`, or `inconclusive`, and every executed case links to
   evidence. Every other status uses `not-run`.
7. **Enforce authorization per case.** Classify the action as read-only,
   authenticated read, reversible state change, state change, active execution,
   high volume, or external contact. Work outside the currently allowed classes
   is marked `requires-separate-approval`; never present it as executable now.
8. **Summarize by family without hiding gaps.** Each family summary references
   all of its coverage records. derive the claim:
   - any evidenced finding → `finding`;
   - any planned or blocked case → `incomplete`;
   - otherwise any inconclusive execution → `inconclusive`;
   - fully executed cases with no findings → `no-issue`;
   - all cases justified as not applicable → `not-applicable`.
9. **Send confirmed vulnerabilities to the reporting skill.** Coverage says
   what was tested. A finding still needs reproducibility, impact, severity, and
   remediation.

## Test depth follows the engagement

- **Completeness does not mean maximum impact.** Cover a high-impact family with
  a blocked or approval-gated record when safe validation is unavailable.
- **Use known fixtures for authorization.** Comparing two supplied accounts is
  evidence; enumerating other customers is scope expansion.
- **State changes need recovery.** Define the exact mutation, expected artifact,
  restoration action, and maximum attempts before seeking approval.
- **Negative bounded tests have limits.** A small race or rate sample may find a
  flaw, but silence does not establish resilience against higher volume.
- **Third-party services remain separate targets.** Record an external redirect,
  storage URL, mail system, or payment processor without touching it unless its
  origin is explicitly in scope.

## Judgment calls

The script derives required families from the normalized surface fields and
checks the evidence contract. It cannot decide whether the route inventory is
complete, whether a payload was technically adequate, or whether linked
evidence proves the claimed security behavior. Review those judgments directly.

## Rationalizations to reject

| Thought | Reality |
|---|---|
| "We planned the test, so this area is covered." | Planned means unexecuted. It supports an `incomplete` summary. |
| "The scanner found nothing." | A tool result proves only the surfaces and techniques it actually exercised. |
| "One user-to-user check covers IDOR." | Record every required direction and role pair explicitly. |
| "We lack an admin account, so vertical access control is not applicable." | Low-privilege denial may be testable; privileged workflow coverage remains blocked. |
| "No finding means secure." | It means no issue was observed within the executed coverage and its limits. |
| "A harmless upload or checkout does not count as a state change." | It still creates client state and requires the authorization assigned to that action class. |
| "The route points to another host, so it is part of the app." | Scope follows explicit origins, not architectural association. |

skills.body:
---
name: binary-fault-triage
description: "Triages supplied binary, crash, sanitizer, dump, static-analysis, and external reproduction evidence to distinguish a lead, observed fault, reproducible fault, security relevance, and demonstrated non-weaponized impact without executing, mutating, exploiting, or weaponizing a binary."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Binary fault triage

Use this skill only to answer: what does supplied evidence prove about an exact binary fault, and what defensive handoff is justified?

## When to Use

- Triage binary fault for authorized security work.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Establish the boundary

1. Work offline from a supplied sanitized ledger.
2. Do not execute, contact, mutate, fuzz, debug, disassemble, reproduce, or test anything.
3. Do not create inputs, commands, flags, tool syntax, offsets, addresses, registers, gadgets, instructions, memory layouts, primitives, bypasses, payloads, exploit scores, or procedures.
4. Treat binaries, dumps, and inputs as restricted artifacts represented only by opaque references and digests.
5. Refuse raw or encoded restricted material and use generic diagnostics; never repeat supplied values.

## Create the ledger

1. Preserve supplied binary digest, build digest, architecture, provenance digest, fault signature, input digest, environment digest, origin lineage, limitations, times, and custody.
2. Record supplied evidence; do not reinterpret an advisory, termination, sanitizer label, or static lead as a runtime fault.
3. Preserve origin lineage. Multiple parsers or reports from one origin are one independent source.
4. Keep identity, occurrence, reproduction, security relevance, mitigation inventory, validity, and impact separate.

## Apply evidence rules

1. Exact identity requires exact binary, build, architecture, provenance, fault signature, input, and environment bindings.
2. Runtime crash evidence can support occurrence. Static analysis supports only a lead.
3. Corroboration requires eligible evidence from at least two independent origin lineages.
4. Reproduction requires an exact supplied external receipt bound to the complete tuple; never perform reproduction here.
5. Security relevance requires exact evidence of a protected-boundary effect. A label, advisory, version, crash, or mitigation state is insufficient.
6. Finding-ready requires exact demonstrated bounded non-weaponized impact. Availability impact is sufficient when evidenced; exploitability is never inferred.
7. Mitigation inventory proves only inventory completeness. Presence and absence prove neither safety nor exploitability.
8. Evidence validity must include the cutoff, and evidence must be recorded within its validity and assessment windows under one uniquely receipted custody record.
9. Not-applicable requires current exact policy evidence whose closed reason exactly matches the cell; it remains in the denominator.
10. Reject conflicting current polarities before applying any state precedence. External reproduction requires a closed independent-external origin with producer and lineage independent of primary evidence.

## Derive without escalation

1. Derive `stale` before all current conclusions.
2. Derive `inconclusive` for mismatched identity or contradictory/insufficient evidence.
3. Derive `finding-ready` only from exact identity, reproduced fault, established relevance, and demonstrated bounded impact.
4. Otherwise derive `security-relevant-fault`, `reproducible-fault`, `observed-fault`, `unsubstantiated-lead`, or `not-security-relevant` from the independent tracks.
5. Never claim control-flow influence, arbitrary read/write, code execution, privilege, sandbox escape, persistence, weaponization, or severity.

## Handoff

1. Use only `evidence-refresh`, `vendor-review`, `remediation-review`, or `validation-readiness`.
2. Apply the closed eligibility matrix: evidence refresh only for lead/inconclusive/stale; vendor review for supported review states; remediation review only for security-relevant or finding-ready; validation readiness only for finding-ready with exact identity, reproduction, relevance, and impact support.
3. Bind a recorded handoff occurrence receipt to its ID, kind, fault, observation, exact evidence set, owner, and time after the observation and every referenced custody receipt.
4. Treat handoffs as defensive coordination, never approval or execution authority.
5. Finding-ready does not create a finding, severity, exploit, or remediation procedure.

## Rationalizations to reject

- “The crash is enough to call it exploitable.” It proves occurrence only.
- “The sanitizer named corruption.” A label is not a protected-boundary effect.
- “The advisory covers this version.” Version matching is not fault identity.
- “Two tools agreed.” Shared lineage is not independent corroboration.
- “The mitigation is absent, so impact is established.” Inventory and impact are independent.
- “Reproduce it quickly to confirm.” This skill never executes or designs reproduction.
- “Include the offset or input for clarity.” Restricted operational material stays outside the ledger.
- “Finding-ready means verified vulnerability.” It means only that bounded, non-weaponized impact evidence is sufficient for a defensive review.

# Binary fault validation readiness

## When to Use

- Checking defensive authority, isolation, budget, stop, cleanup, custody, and independent-review readiness without analyzing faults, creating tests or inputs, determining exploitability, or authorizing execution or development.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Purpose

Validate a supplied closed readiness ledger and produce, at most, a
non-authorizing handoff for separate isolated validation review. A complete
ledger establishes internal consistency only; it does not approve, perform, or
describe validation.

## Boundary

Never inspect or analyze a binary fault. Never execute, mutate, fuzz, debug,
disassemble, reproduce, or validate anything. Never create a test, input,
exploit, payload, proof of concept, command, pseudocode, debugger syntax,
address, offset, register, instruction, gadget, memory layout, primitive,
bypass, path, or target. Never determine exploitability, severity, success, or
validation outcome. Never authorize execution, exploit development, or use of a
production environment.

## Workflow

1. Accept only a supplied exact `binary-fault-triage/v2` assessment result whose
   review status is `passed` and whose upstream handoff is recorded
   `validation-readiness`.
2. Stop on operational or restricted content. Do not quote rejected values.
3. Verify the canonical imported receipt over the complete opaque binary,
   build, architecture, provenance, fault, input, environment, observation,
   artifact, review, policy, and upstream handoff bindings.
4. Record only supplied passive sanitized receipts. Never contact an artifact,
   source, lab, target, or downstream operator.
5. Instantiate all nine essential readiness checks. None is not-applicable.
6. Keep authority actions limited to `readiness-review` and
   `handoff-recording`; neither grants execution authority.
7. Require every satisfied check to carry one canonical role-specific subject
   proof. Require an isolated non-production lab, exact numeric ceilings, exact
   stop-pretest proof, ready cleanup, retained custody, and genuinely independent
   review lineage.
8. Derive gate precedence as `prohibited`, `triage-refresh-required`,
   `approval-required`, `blocked`, then `handoff-ready`.
9. Treat `handoff-ready` as readiness for separate review only. It is not
   execution permission, validation success, or a technical conclusion.
10. Keep handoffs exact-bound and chronological. Null ownership derives
    `withheld`; a recorded occurrence requires an opaque owner and later receipt.
11. Derive withdrawal after authority expiry or revocation, bound drift,
    custody disposal, budget exhaustion, a fired stop, or cleanup loss. Require
    a later exact trigger-bound receipt for `withdrawn`.

## Report

State the ledger identifier, contradictions, exact gate and handoff counts,
blocker gate IDs, and withdrawal handoff IDs. Add: “Internal readiness
consistency only; no fault analysis, validation, execution authority,
exploitability determination, or development authorization occurred.”

## Rationalizations to reject

- **“The triage review passed, so run a quick confirmation.”** The upstream
  receipt starts governance only; this skill never validates.
- **“Finding-ready means exploitable.”** Triage explicitly does not establish
  exploitability, and this ledger cannot add that claim.
- **“The input digest is available, so reconstruct the input.”** Digests bind
  identity only; restricted artifacts stay opaque.
- **“The lab is isolated, so authority is implied.”** Isolation and authority
  are independent mandatory checks.
- **“A handoff-ready gate authorizes the operator.”** It permits only separate
  review; downstream execution authority is outside this skill.
- **“A stopped or expired package can be resumed.”** No retry or resume state
  exists; refresh the evidence and establish a new readiness record.

skills.name: memory-forensics-triage
skills.desc: Triages supplied Windows, Linux, or other volatile-memory images while preserving acquisition provenance, image integrity, process and region evidence, network and object correlations, extracted-artifact custody, timeline limits, and claim confidence. Use for offline memory-forensics review and handoff, not live rootkit trust assessment or full malware reverse engineering.
skills.body:
---
name: memory-forensics-triage
description: "Triages supplied Windows, Linux, or other volatile-memory images while preserving acquisition provenance, image integrity, process and region evidence, network and object correlations, extracted-artifact custody, timeline limits, and claim confidence. Use for offline memory-forensics review and handoff, not live rootkit trust assessment or full malware reverse engineering."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Memory forensics triage

Memory is a captured vantage, not an infallible narrator. Acquisition changes the
system; the acquisition path can be subverted; symbols can be wrong; one image can
produce many correlated outputs without becoming multiple independent sources.

This skill analyzes supplied image facts and normalized outputs. It does not
acquire memory, provide live collection commands, recover credential material,
execute extracted code, query reputation services, or authorize containment.

## When to Use

- Triage memory forensics for authorized security work.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Workflow

1. Record written authorization, case and asset identity, platform, image name,
   size, format, acquisition method and window, tool identity, hash, transfer,
   custodian, storage, access-log state, acquisition impact, and clock basis.
2. Record the analysis engine, version, reported platform or build, selected
   symbols or profile, match state, validation evidence, and limitations. A
   successful plugin run does not prove the profile is correct.
3. Inventory each supplied observation with its image, source group, artifact
   class, locator, role, honest time precision, and limitations. Different
   plugins over one image share one source group.
4. Correlate process inventory and lineage, executable regions, modules or
   mappings, network objects, handles, registry objects, files, credentials,
   kernel or driver structures, and supplied baselines. Preserve benign
   alternatives and missing cross-vantage evidence.
5. Keep claim types narrow. A connection is a network object, not C2 attribution.
   An LSASS handle is credential access capability, not credential extraction. A
   Run value is a persistence mechanism, not proof it executed.
6. Use `suspicious` for mutually reinforcing indicators within one source group.
   Use `corroborated` only with at least two independent source groups. Use
   `confirmed` only when the claim-specific proof requirements in
7. Track every candidate extraction. `extracted` needs a preserved digest and
   custody. Malware classification needs analysis of the extracted artifact;
   bytes that were never recovered cannot be classified.
8. Build timeline events only from cited times. Keep host-clock time separate
   from trusted time; unknown skew remains a limitation. Do not assign an exact
   timestamp to an object merely because the image has an acquisition window.
9. Cover all required artifact and case categories. Mark missing work `blocked`
   with a blocker rather than calling the surface clean.
10. Record owned, authorization-aware next steps and handoffs. Contact with a
    live host or external service needs explicit authority beyond offline review.

## Boundary with adjacent skills

- Use `rootkit-triage` when live host views may be lying and the task is to
  compare kernel, boot, firmware, memory, disk, and external vantages.
- Use `protocol-traffic-analysis` for packet-capture interpretation.
- Use `credential-exposure-audit` for credential-material inventory and handling.
- Hand extracted binaries to a malware or binary-analysis workflow; this skill
  preserves extraction provenance and the questions to answer.
- Use `detection-engineering` to turn stable observations into detector logic.
- Use `findings-report` for final stakeholder finding prose.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **"Several plugins agree, so the finding is independently corroborated."**
  Plugins reading one image share acquisition and parsing dependencies.
- **"RWX plus an MZ header proves malware."** Legitimate software and injected
  security components can create similar regions; preserve and analyze the bytes.
- **"Port 443 from a suspicious process is C2."** The memory object proves a
  connection, not destination ownership, protocol content, or intent.
- **"A handle to LSASS proves credentials were stolen."** Access capability is
  not proof that credential material was read or used.
- **"A Run value proves persistence succeeded."** It proves a mechanism was
  represented in memory; execution and durable disk state need more evidence.
- **"The image hash makes acquisition trustworthy."** It protects the captured
  file after hashing; it does not validate the acquisition binary or compromised
  source path.
- **"Exact plugin timestamps are trusted UTC."** They remain host-clock values
  until clock basis and skew are established.

# Rootkit triage

A suspected rootkit changes the reliability of the instrument used to inspect
it. Treat live host output as one view, preserve provenance, and seek evidence
from a different or lower trust layer before strengthening the claim.

This skill decides whether rootkit suspicion is unsupported, suspected,
corroborated, or confirmed; what to preserve; and what containment or specialist
handoff is justified. It does not perform full memory reconstruction, develop or
deploy a rootkit, or prescribe live deletion from a system whose kernel or boot
chain may be compromised.

## When to Use

- Host tools may be lying and the incident needs evidence-preserving cross-view analysis, containment, or forensic handoff.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Workflow

1. Record the asset, platform, authorization, business context, current
   isolation state, and suspected layers: userland, kernel, eBPF or driver,
   boot, hypervisor, or firmware.
2. Inventory supplied evidence with its source, locator, acquisition time or
   bounded window, vantage, role, and integrity hash where the evidence record requires
   one. Do not invent acquisition precision.
3. Assign trust from vantage rather than tool reputation. Live OS output is low
   trust for rootkit absence; external network observations and offline disk are
   medium; offline memory, hardware attestation, and external firmware reads are
   high.
4. Compare independent views of processes, files, network activity, modules or
   drivers, hooks, eBPF state, boot measurements, firmware, and timing. Two tools
   that depend on the same live kernel do not form an independent cross-view.
5. Build hypotheses from evidence and comparisons. A discrepancy supports
   suspicion. Corroboration needs independent vantage groups. Confirmation needs
   a high-trust direct artifact, an independent supporting vantage, and a
   discrepancy tied to the claim.
6. Cover case context, preservation, process, file, network, module or driver,
   control-flow hook, eBPF, boot, firmware or hypervisor, memory, and containment
   questions. Keep unavailable layers blocked rather than clean.
7. Plan preservation before reboot, artifact removal, rebuild, or firmware
   changes. Record authorization and evidence impact on every action. A review
   pass is not permission to execute it.
8. Choose containment from the evidence strength and business impact. Preserve
   volatile evidence when feasible, isolate confirmed or corroborated cases,
   and use trusted-media rebuild or hardware escalation when the affected trust
   layer makes live cleanup unreliable.
9. Hand detailed memory reconstruction to a memory-forensics workflow. Hand
   firmware acquisition to a hardware or firmware workflow. Keep the triage
   record as the chain between the initial discrepancy and those analyses.

## Interpretation rules

- Agreement among live tools is weak evidence because they may share the same
  compromised API, kernel structure, or hook.
- A cross-view discrepancy is an indicator. Benign races, collection timing,
  permissions, parsing, and normal updates remain alternative explanations.
- A matching boot measurement is evidence about measured components and the
  referenced baseline. It does not clear unmeasured firmware or runtime state.
- A memory image acquired through the suspected kernel can still be manipulated.
  Record the acquisition vantage and preserve that limitation.
- A valid signature establishes signer and file integrity, not benign behavior.
- If kernel, boot, hypervisor, or firmware compromise is confirmed, restoration
  from trusted media and re-attestation are usually more defensible than live
  artifact deletion.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **"Every live tool agrees, so the host is clean."** Shared dependence on the
  same compromised layer can make agreement systematic deception.
- **"A discrepancy proves a rootkit."** Collection races, permissions, parsing,
  and legitimate changes must remain visible until independent evidence resolves them.
- **"The scanner named a rootkit family."** Signature output is a lead until its
  matched artifact and provenance are preserved and examined.
- **"Reboot first and see if it goes away."** Reboot destroys volatile evidence
  and can activate boot persistence or recovery behavior.
- **"We found the file, so delete it now."** Live removal can destroy evidence,
  trigger defensive behavior, or leave the lower trust layer compromised.
- **"Secure Boot passed, so firmware is fine."** Attestation covers the measured
  chain and baseline; it does not establish every firmware component is benign.

skills.name: defensive-control-evidence-synthesis
skills.desc: Synthesizes supplied evidence-backed defensive assessment results and administrative receipts into a scope-bound control-evidence matrix that preserves lineage, freshness, contradictions, unknowns, and gaps. Use when consolidating defensive control evidence without scanning, scoring, certifying, or rewriting findings.
skills.body:
---
name: defensive-control-evidence-synthesis
description: "Synthesizes supplied evidence-backed defensive assessment results and administrative receipts into a scope-bound control-evidence matrix that preserves lineage, freshness, contradictions, unknowns, and gaps. Use when consolidating defensive control evidence without scanning, scoring, certifying, or rewriting findings."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Defensive control evidence synthesis

## When to Use

- Consolidating defensive control evidence without scanning, scoring, certifying, or rewriting findings.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Purpose

Build and validate a closed matrix from already-supplied specialist artifacts
and sanitized administrative, validation, or remediation-verification receipts.

## Boundary

Never contact a system, scan, sample, query, test, or execute. Reject raw logs,
configurations, ACLs, credentials, tickets, certificates, packets, live
identifiers, commands, queries, rules, test bodies, attack paths, and remediation
procedures. Never create, rewrite, merge, close, or severity-rank findings.
Never calculate a posture score, grade, maturity level, compliance result,
certification, or exploitability rank.

## Workflow

1. Accept only exact passed specialist artifacts and sanitized administrative,
   validation, or remediation-verification receipts already supplied.
2. Stop on operational or restricted content. Do not quote rejected values.
3. Preserve producer, artifact format, artifact digest, review receipt, scope,
   policy, time, window, origin lineage, upstream class, polarity, limitations,
   applicability, and strength.
4. Report only generic diagnostic codes; never reflect restricted values.
5. Keep all ten policy dimensions in the exact scope-by-dimension denominator.
6. Do not strengthen, reverse, or reinterpret an upstream claim. Preserve or
   weaken it only when freshness or custody requires that result.
7. Cap administrative evidence at `documented` or `configured`.
8. Treat a review pass as artifact-structure evidence, not proof of no exposure
   or proof that a control works.
9. Keep telemetry, detection, containment, and recovery evidence independent.
10. Accept a no-finding claim only from exact, complete, current upstream
    coverage.
11. Deduplicate shared origin lineage before assessing independence.
12. Require one open contradiction for eligible opposing independent claims.
13. Use `not-applicable` only when source, claim, binding, and cell carry the
    same exact current policy reason.
14. Require one immutable finding reference for each current or stale,
    otherwise-valid exposure claim; do not edit the upstream finding.
15. Treat remediation occurrence as unverified until a later exact verification
    receipt independently binds the earlier occurrence, scope, and dimension.
16. Keep evidence gaps administrative. They are not technical findings.
17. Keep handoffs exact-bound, chronological, defensive, and non-authorizing.
18. Return exact state counts, contradiction IDs, gap IDs, and finding-reference
    IDs. Never produce a score.

## Report

State the matrix identifier, exact state counts, contradictions, evidence gaps,
and immutable finding references. Add: “Internal synthesis consistency only; no
live interaction, score, compliance determination, certification, or finding
modification occurred.”

## Rationalizations to reject

- **“The record is complete, so there is no exposure.”** Completeness validates
  the supplied artifact contract, not the absence of findings.
- **“Configured means validated.”** Administrative receipts cannot prove
  observation or validation.
- **“Telemetry means detection.”** Collection evidence does not prove a
  detection outcome.
- **“Detection means containment or recovery.”** These are separate claims.
- **“Two copies are independent.”** Shared origin lineage is one source.
- **“Implementation closed the gap.”** Occurrence is not later verification.
- **“A score makes this easier.”** Aggregation would erase unknowns and disputes.
- **“We can clean up upstream findings.”** This skill never rewrites them.
