skills.name: detection-engineering
skills.desc: Builds detection rules that are proven before they ship — fire on known-bad, stay silent on known-good — and keeps false positives from blinding the SOC. Use when writing a Sigma/Suricata/YARA rule, reviewing a detection before deployment, triaging alert fatigue, or deciding whether a rule has earned production.
skills.body:
---
name: detection-engineering
description: "Builds detection rules that are proven before they ship — fire on known-bad, stay silent on known-good — and keeps false positives from blinding the SOC. Use when writing a Sigma/Suricata/YARA rule, reviewing a detection before deployment, triaging alert fatigue, or deciding whether a rule has earned production."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob Bash
---

# Detection engineering

A detection rule is a claim: *this pattern means an attack*. The claim is worth
nothing until it has been tested both ways.

**Every rule must pass two tests, and neither substitutes for the other:**

- **Fires on known-bad** — it actually triggered on a true-positive sample.
- **Silent on known-good** — it did *not* trigger on a benign sample.

A rule tested only against the attack is unproven against false positives. A
rule never tested against the attack is unproven, period. If you cannot show
both for a rule in production, you have a rule collection, not a detection
programme.

## When to Use

- Writing a Sigma/Suricata/YARA rule, reviewing a detection before deployment, triaging alert fatigue, or deciding whether a rule has earned production.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Prove it before it ships

```sh
uv run {baseDir}/scripts/check_detection.py record.json
```

Takes a test record per rule and fails any rule missing either proof, firing on
known-good, over the false-positive ceiling, or unmapped to an ATT&CK
technique. Exit `0` only when every rule is proven both ways; `1` on any
unproven rule; `2` on empty input. See `references/test-record.md`.

## Production decision

| Known-bad result | Known-good result | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fires | Silent | Eligible for controlled rollout |
| Fires | Fires | Rewrite or narrowly tune; false-positive proof failed |
| Silent | Silent | Do not ship; the rule did not detect the behavior |
| Missing | Any result | Unproven; collect the missing test evidence |
| Fires | Silent, but provenance or mapping missing | Hold until the rule can support a defensible coverage claim |

Record the decision per rule. A passing rule does not prove that the production
pipeline will deliver or alert on it; live validation belongs to
`detection-validate`.

## False positives are the silent killer

Analysts go alert-blind within weeks when most of what fires is garbage — then
the real alert gets the same shrug. Manage it in this order:

1. **Baseline first.** Run a new rule in detection-only mode for ~2 weeks. Count
   the fires, investigate a sample, learn what normal looks like.
2. **Exception lists, not rule disablement.** If a rule is noisy on one service
   account, exclude that account — do not switch the rule off for everyone.
3. **Track the rate.** Above ~90% false positives the logic is wrong, not the
   exceptions. Rewrite it; do not tune it.

## Every rule carries its provenance

For each rule you should be able to answer: where did the idea come from, what
threat it addresses, what log source powers it, when it was last tested, and
its false-positive rate. A rule whose last test date is unknown is an unproven
rule regardless of how long it has been deployed — time in production is not
evidence.

## Keep detections in version control

Rules in Git, tests beside them, CI that validates syntax and runs each rule
against sample known-bad and known-good log data before it compiles to your
SIEM format. A detection pipeline without a test step ships unproven rules by
construction.

## Rationalizations to reject

| Rationalization | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| “The attack sample fired, so the rule can ship.” | It remains unproven against false positives; the SOC goes blind |
| “It has been in production for a year, so it works.” | Time deployed is not a test. If the last-tested date is unknown, the rule is unproven |
| “The rule is noisy, so disable it.” | Disabling it loses the true positives with the false ones; use a bounded exception instead |
| “We can tune around a 95% false-positive rate.” | The logic is wrong, not the thresholds — rewrite it |
| “ATT&CK mapping is optional documentation.” | Without the mapping, the rule cannot support a defensible coverage claim |

## References

- [Test record format](references/test-record.md) — the JSON the checker consumes, and what each field proves

skills.desc: Plans and records bounded defensive tests of whether preventive controls, telemetry, and detections remain effective across pre-approved opaque technique variations. Use when a blue or purple team needs authorization-, safety-, evidence-, cleanup-, and remediation-gated resilience measurement without generating bypass procedures, commands, payloads, or stealth rankings.
skills.body:
---
name: detection-resilience-test-plan
description: "Plans and records bounded defensive tests of whether preventive controls, telemetry, and detections remain effective across pre-approved opaque technique variations. Use when a blue or purple team needs authorization-, safety-, evidence-, cleanup-, and remediation-gated resilience measurement without generating bypass procedures, commands, payloads, or stealth rankings."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Detection resilience test plan

Measure whether a particular defensive environment prevents, observes, and
detects a pre-approved synthetic test. Keep those claims separate and bind them
to evidence, an exact environment fingerprint, and an expiry window. A finding
of a real control gap is a useful result; fabricated coverage is not.

## When to Use

- A blue or purple team needs authorization-, safety-, evidence-, cleanup-, and remediation-gated resilience measurement without generating bypass procedures, commands, payloads, or stealth rankings.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Boundary

Consume externally supplied fixtures by opaque ID and SHA-256 digest only.
Never create, transform, reconstruct, rank, or recommend a fixture or technique
implementation. Record only bounded defensive facts and approved receipts.
Use only the contract's bounded declarative grammar in descriptions and rationale;
arbitrary prose, imperatives, and comparative rankings cannot be recorded.

Version 0.1 permits `isolated-lab` and `dedicated-test-tenant` environments.
Production execution is prohibited. Do not include hostnames, addresses,
domains, accounts, paths, tenant names, organizations, credentials, client data,
or malware. Scope identifiers are opaque; evidence locators are opaque references.

Do not supply source code, pseudocode, operational commands, flags, payloads,
build instructions, mutation, encoding, packing, obfuscation, signature-avoidance,
loader guidance, injection, in-memory execution, syscall, sandbox-detection,
inspection bypass, security-tool disablement, or telemetry-blinding procedures.
Do not supply C2 profiles, jitter, protocol mimicry, fronting, traffic shaping,
product-specific working bypasses, stealth scores, likelihoods, rankings, or
deployment advice. A request for any of these cannot be fulfilled by this skill.

## Workflow

1. **Declare authority before planning attempts.** Start from an external
   authorization artifact bound to exact scope units, environment profiles,
   fixtures, action classes, operators, windows, and budgets. Placeholders are
   not approvals. Missing authority is a blocker, never implied permission.

2. **Pin isolation and the defensive environment.** Record the isolated
   environment class and broad scope categories. Bind immutable receipts for
   the platform, control product, engine, content, policy, analytic package,
   time synchronization, and rollback baseline. Drift makes prior results
   historical rather than current coverage.

3. **Reference approved opaque fixtures and declare hypotheses.** Record the
   supplier receipt, digest, integrity proof, synthetic provenance, taxonomy
   reference, benign effect class, and semantic-equivalence evidence. Define
   each hypothesis before execution for one exact fixture, environment, and
   scope tuple. A hypothesis says what to measure; it cannot predict the result.

4. **Declare readiness, budgets, and stop controls.** Bind per-case and aggregate
   attempt, duration, state-change, and signal ceilings. Name the stop owner and
   pretest evidence. Unexpected impact, telemetry loss, scope drift, exhausted
   budget, or lost rollback readiness requires stopping. There is no resume path
   within a stopped attempt; retry requires a new approval gate.

5. **Record supplied attempt facts within that envelope.** This skill records
   authorized execution performed through an external approved process; it does
   not execute or provide that process. Preserve failed, blocked, and stopped
   attempts. A retry is a new attempt and cannot borrow a previous result.

6. **Keep evidence roles distinct.** Record prevention response, benign effect,
   telemetry baseline and field availability, query completion and window, and
   alert outcome separately. Silence supports `not-detected` only with healthy
   telemetry and a complete query spanning the attempt; otherwise it is
   `inconclusive`.

7. **Preserve custody and prove cleanup.** Bind each evidence artifact to one
   terminal custody record, including artifacts unused in claims. Keep stale,
   unavailable, disposed, future, cross-scope, and tuple-mismatched evidence out
   of current claims. Cleanup completion requires causally later exact proof and
   never authorizes disposal of retained defender evidence.

8. **Record gaps, remediation, and the whole coverage universe.** Bind each gap
   to exact support and an owner. An implemented change is not verified
   remediation without a later bounded retest. Keep every hypothesis and
   applicable control-layer cell in the denominator, including planned,
   blocked, prohibited, stopped, inconclusive, excluded, and gap cases.

9. **Derive states from the supplied record.** Apply the declared precedence and
   evidence-role rules consistently to readiness, attempt, prevention,
   detection, benign effect, combined outcome, validity, cleanup, gaps, and
   remediation. Leave claims unresolved when required facts are unavailable. A
   complete record grants no execution authority and proves no deployment safety.

10. **Hand off the evidence-bound result.** Report current versus stale outcomes,
    blockers, gaps, budget consumption, cleanup failures, remediation state, and
    required owners. Keep unknown prerequisites, field availability, telemetry
    health, and incomplete queries visible; never invent receipts or measurements.

## Boundary with adjacent skills

- `detection-validate` owns broader post-exercise technique coverage; export only

skills.name: detection-validate
skills.desc: Runs attacker techniques and confirms whether detections actually fire, producing an honest ATT&CK coverage map that separates real gaps from accepted ones. Use when running a purple-team exercise, measuring detection coverage, validating that a SOC can see a technique, or turning 'we think we're covered' into evidence per technique.
skills.body:
---
name: detection-validate
description: "Runs attacker techniques and confirms whether detections actually fire, producing an honest ATT&CK coverage map that separates real gaps from accepted ones. Use when running a purple-team exercise, measuring detection coverage, validating that a SOC can see a technique, or turning 'we think we're covered' into evidence per technique."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob Bash
---

# Detection validation

Purple team answers one question, per technique: we executed it — did a
detection fire? Everything else is commentary.

**"We think we're covered" is not coverage.** Coverage is a specific claim
about specific techniques, backed by a recorded outcome for each. A map with
blanks in the detection column is the same lie as a port scan that came back
clean with zero coverage — a confident summary over an unanswered question.

## When to Use

- Running a purple-team exercise, measuring detection coverage, validating that a SOC can see a technique, or turning 'we think we're covered' into evidence per technique.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Every executed technique gets exactly one honest outcome

| Outcome | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `covered` | executed, a detection fired |
| `partial` | fired weakly, or on only some variants |
| `not-detected` | executed, nothing fired — **a real gap** |
| `not-detectable` | passive technique with no observable (OSINT, reading public records) — **an accepted gap, not a failure** |
| `unknown` | executed but the outcome was never recorded — **the one that poisons the report** |

The distinction that matters: `not-detectable` is honest (you looked, there is
nothing to see, you accept it) while `unknown` is a blank wearing a confident
coverage number. They must never be conflated.

## Score the map

```sh
uv run {baseDir}/scripts/coverage_map.py map.json
```

Computes real coverage as covered+partial over everything executed that *could*
be detected — passive `not-detectable` techniques are removed from the
denominator. Exit `0` only when every executed technique has a known, non-gap
outcome; `1` when any `not-detected` or `unknown` remains; `2` on bad or empty
input. See `references/coverage-map.md`.

## Validation record

For each technique, return the technique and variant, execution receipt,
expected observable, telemetry-health evidence, alert evidence, one outcome
from the table above, limitations, and an owner for any gap. Keep the execution
receipt and alert receipt separate: the same timestamp or operator note cannot
prove both sides of the join.

End with counts for `covered`, `partial`, `not-detected`, `not-detectable`, and
`unknown`, plus the denominator used. Never publish only a percentage.

## Pair with the attacker and the detector

This skill is the join between offense and defense:

- The offensive technique comes from the operator (or an attack simulation). If
  you cannot execute it, you cannot validate its detection — an untested
  technique is `unknown`, never assume `covered`.
- The detection that should fire is engineered and proven separately. A rule
  that passed its own true-positive test in isolation can still fail to fire in
  a live exercise against the real technique variant — that is exactly what this
  measures, and why the exercise is not redundant with the rule's unit test.

## Rationalizations to reject

| Thought | Reality |
|---|---|
| "We ran 40 techniques, we're covered." | Not until all 40 have a recorded outcome. Blanks are `unknown`, and unknown is not coverage. |
| "No alert fired, so the technique must be benign." | No alert fired means you did not detect it. That is a gap, not an all-clear. |
| "It's probably detected, the rule exists." | A rule existing is not a rule firing. The exercise exists because rules fail live that passed in isolation. |
| "Mark the passive stuff as covered so the number looks complete." | `not-detectable` is removed from the denominator, not counted as covered. Honest beats complete. |
| "We'll fill in the blanks later." | A blank is `unknown` now. Ship the map honest with the gaps visible, or re-run the technique. |
| "100% coverage." | Almost always means the un-run techniques were left off the map. Coverage is over what you executed, and the map must show what you did not. |

## References

- [Coverage map format](references/coverage-map.md) — the JSON the scorer consumes, the five outcomes, and how the denominator is computed

# Incident validation correlation

## When to Use

- Correlate incident evidence with validation results.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Purpose

Answer one question: is an exact, pre-approved isolated validation genuinely
comparable to a supplied sanitized incident observation, and what defensive
learning survives? A complete ledger does not close an incident, verify
remediation, establish attribution or scope, or prove coverage.

## Boundary

Never contact assets, identities, sources, responders, or attackers. Never hunt,
respond, validate production, design or execute techniques, author detections,
manage cases, create findings, or write reports. Reject hostnames, addresses,
accounts, tenants, domains, paths, victim identities, IOCs, raw events, packets,
memory, malware, credentials, tickets, certificates, commands, scripts, queries,
rules, payloads, technique procedures, tool syntax, infrastructure, and
operational timelines. Use sanitized opaque references and digests only.

## Workflow

1. Accept only supplied incident packages and supplied, immutable,
   pre-approved validation cases and receipts.
2. Stop on restricted content. Never quote a rejected value.
3. Preserve separate incident acceptance and validation execution authority.
4. Report only generic diagnostic codes; never reflect restricted values.
5. Require exactly one observation and one pre-approved case for each supplied
   learning item and objective.
6. Require observation time before learning creation and independent validation
    approval after learning creation.
7. Require exact semantic-equivalence binding across observation class,
    immutable fixture, objective, environment limitations, and expected benign
    effect. Taxonomy similarity is not equivalence.
8. Mark weak equivalence `not-comparable`. Never claim that a lab reproduces a
    production incident or that production predicts lab behavior.
9. Keep prevent, observe, detect, contain, and recover comparisons separate.
10. Keep observation, execution, benign-effect, telemetry, alert, containment,
    recovery, cleanup, custody, and policy evidence roles separate. Require the
    closed role/outcome matrix; labels never override contradictory evidence.
    Consume every supplied authority and environment exactly once.
11. An alert is not complete telemetry or control evidence. A validation alert
    is not incident reproduction.
12. Treat alert absence under unhealthy telemetry as `inconclusive`.
13. Accept only isolated-lab or dedicated-test-tenant validation receipts.
14. Treat a fired stop as terminal. Allow only later cleanup, custody, and
    withdrawal; retry needs a new separately approved case.
    Authority expiry, revocation, fixture drift, and environment drift are also
    terminal: no later execution, evidence, or result is valid.
15. Require exact current policy proof and a closed NA reason code for
    not-applicable. Keep every objective in the denominator.
16. Keep handoff occurrence, approval, authority, result, and withdrawal
    separate with typed exact receipts. Expiry, revocation, fixture drift,
    environment drift, and a fired stop require withdrawal. A handoff never
    grants authority. Custody precedes every consuming result, gap, or handoff
    receipt; withdrawal evidence is exact for its trigger.
17. Interpret `complete` as correlation complete only. Never call the incident
    closed or remediation verified.
18. Return comparison states, cycle states, learning-gap IDs, and handoff states.
    Never assign severity, compliance, or detection coverage.

## Report

State the ledger identifier, exact objective denominator, comparison and cycle
counts, learning gaps, and handoff states. Add: “Correlation consistency only;
no live interaction, incident closure, remediation verification, attribution,
severity, or coverage claim occurred.”

## Rationalizations to reject

- **“The taxonomy matches.”** Similar labels do not establish equivalence.
- **“The lab reproduced production.”** Environment limits survive correlation.
- **“The alert proves detection.”** Alert evidence is only one role.
- **“No alert means a gap.”** Unhealthy telemetry makes the result inconclusive.
- **“The stop cleared, so retry.”** A stop is terminal for that approved case.
- **“Cleanup means validation succeeded.”** Cleanup proves only cleanup.
- **“The handoff approved execution.”** Handoffs transfer defensive learning only.
- **“Complete means the incident is closed.”** It means correlation complete.

# Telemetry coverage audit

## When to Use

- Reviewing evidence quality or profile-specific telemetry usability without contacting sources or claiming detection coverage.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Purpose

Validate an already-supplied passive evidence ledger. A complete review means
only that the ledger is internally consistent with supplied policy. It does not prove
detection coverage, effectiveness, activity absence, or operational readiness.

## Boundary

skills.body:
---
name: agent-action-proof
description: "Grades evidence for an AI agent's downstream actions without overstating what a callback, tool trace, file read, command result, or target change proves. Use when validating impact, writing findings, or reviewing agent test receipts."
metadata:
  portability: universal
  discipline: engagement-operations
  domain: ai-systems
  tags: [agents, evidence, impact, provenance, reporting]
---

# Agent action proof

Determine the strongest claim supported by an agent test receipt. Keep model
output, tool invocation, target-side effect, and business impact distinct.

## When to Use

- Reviewing evidence from an authorized agent or tool-use assessment.
- Deciding whether a result proves instruction acceptance, tool use, target
  action, or demonstrated impact.
- Preparing a reproducible finding or validation handoff.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not use this skill to execute the action being evaluated.
- Do not promote screenshots, model narration, or a callback alone into proof
  of target-side execution.
- Do not preserve secrets or sensitive output in the report when a restricted
  evidence reference is sufficient.

## Evidence ladder

Use the highest rung supported by independent receipts:

1. `presented` — the instruction or data reached the model context.
2. `accepted` — the model output adopted or repeated the requested intent.
3. `tool-selected` — the agent requested a named tool with recorded arguments.
4. `tool-invoked` — the runtime dispatched the request to the tool boundary.
5. `target-observed` — target-origin evidence shows the requested read, write,
   query, or operation occurred.
6. `effect-verified` — a separately observed target state changed as expected.
7. `impact-demonstrated` — the bounded effect reached the stated security or
   business consequence.

Never collapse rungs. A DNS or HTTP callback is interaction evidence; a file
read is not command execution; command execution is not elevated execution; an
attempted write is not a durable state change.

## Workflow

1. Record the authorization reference, exact target, test identity, environment,
   time window, approved action class, disruption limit, and cleanup duty.
2. Assign a unique run identifier and carry it through model, runtime, tool,
   target, and cleanup records.
3. Preserve the original artifacts. Record origin, collector, timestamp, target
   identity, resource identity, integrity value where available, and access
   restrictions.
4. Reconstruct the chain chronologically: input, model response, agent decision,
   tool request, runtime dispatch, tool result, target observation, state check,
   and cleanup receipt.
5. Mark each link `present`, `missing`, `contradicted`, or `not-applicable`.
   Correlation by time alone is not identity proof.
6. Place the result on the evidence ladder. State the missing receipt required
   for the next rung.
7. Check alternative explanations: synthetic tool output, replayed callback,
   cached data, a different identity, pre-existing state, race conditions, or
   operator action outside the agent path.
8. Separate severity from proof. Severity may consider the demonstrated
   consequence and preconditions, but it cannot strengthen the evidence chain.
9. Confirm cleanup from target-origin state where cleanup was required. Record
   residual artifacts and failed rollback explicitly.

## Deliverable

Return the bounded claim, achieved evidence rung, receipt chain, missing and
contradictory links, alternative explanations, identity and timestamp limits,
cleanup status, and the exact additional evidence needed to strengthen the
claim.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **“The agent said it succeeded.”** Model narration is not a target receipt.
- **“The tool returned success.”** Tool output can be wrong, spoofed, cached, or
  disconnected from the intended target.
- **“The callback proves code execution.”** It proves only the observed
  interaction unless a stronger target-side receipt exists.
- **“The timestamps line up.”** Temporal correlation does not prove identity or
  causation.
- **“The impact is obvious from the primitive.”** Report the demonstrated
  effect and keep downstream consequences as bounded analysis.
- **“Cleanup probably happened when the session ended.”** Cleanup needs its own
  receipt when state could persist.

skills.body:
---
name: ai-threat-model
description: "Builds an evidence-bound AI threat model from partial architecture, trust, identity, data-flow, and control information. Use when scoping an AI assessment, reviewing a design, or prioritizing realistic attack paths under uncertainty."
metadata:
  portability: universal
  discipline: engagement-operations
  domain: ai-systems
  tags: [ai, threat-modeling, architecture, trust-boundaries, risk]
---

# AI threat model

Turn incomplete system knowledge into a decision-ready threat model without
inventing architecture. Preserve uncertainty as a first-class result and update
the model when evidence changes.

## When to Use

- Scoping an AI security review or penetration test.
- Reviewing a design that combines models, retrieval, agents, tools, data, and
  conventional application or cloud services.
- Prioritizing assessment paths when architecture evidence is incomplete or
  contradictory.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat the model as permission to validate a threat on a live target.
- Do not use a generic AI risk list in place of the system's actual boundaries.
- Do not assign likelihood or impact precision unsupported by evidence.

## Workflow

1. State the decision the threat model must support, the assessment scope, and
   the evidence cutoff date.
2. Build an assumption register. For every unknown needed to continue, record
   the assumption, why it matters, the evidence that would resolve it, its
   owner, and the consequence if it is false.
3. Identify crown jewels and safety properties. Include sensitive data,
   model behavior, tool authority, workload identity, evaluation integrity,
   deployment artifacts, human approvals, and availability where relevant.
4. Map components and trust zones. Include users, applications, model gateways,
   model providers, retrieval pipelines, agent runtimes, tools, memory,
   registries, CI/CD, monitoring, and administrative planes.
5. Draw data, instruction, identity, and artifact flows separately. A component
   can trust data but not instructions, or accept an artifact without loading it.
6. For each boundary, ask what can cross, who authorizes it, which identity is
   used, what validation occurs, what logs survive, and what downstream
   consumer acts on the result.
7. Construct attack-path hypotheses from evidence-backed transitions. Label
   every step `observed`, `assumed`, `inferred`, or `blocked`; one unknown step
   prevents the full path from being called demonstrated.
8. Evaluate threats across the AI-specific surfaces:
   - instruction and context control;
   - retrieval and knowledge integrity;
   - agent and tool authority;
   - model and artifact supply chain;
   - identity and secret propagation;
   - output consumption and automation;
   - monitoring, evaluation, and human oversight.
9. Prioritize by plausible consequence, exposed preconditions, boundary count,
   control evidence, and uncertainty. Do not multiply arbitrary numbers to
   manufacture precision.
10. Convert priorities into bounded review questions, control gaps, evidence
    requests, and separately authorized validation objectives.
11. Version the model. Record which new evidence confirmed, weakened, blocked,
    or split each path.

## Deliverable

Return a threat-model package containing the system purpose, scope, evidence
cutoff, crown jewels, component and trust-zone map, separated flow maps,
assumption register, attack-path hypotheses, control observations, prioritized
review questions, and change log.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **“This is a standard RAG architecture.”** Shared labels do not prove shared
  trust boundaries or controls.
- **“The diagram is authoritative because the client supplied it.”** Supplied
  architecture is reported evidence and may be stale.
- **“An assumed step is probably true, so the path is complete.”** A path is no
  stronger than its weakest unsupported transition.
- **“Map every framework technique.”** Exhaustive taxonomy mapping can obscure
  the system-specific decisions the model exists to support.
- **“A low likelihood makes the control gap unimportant.”** Weak evidence for
  likelihood should remain uncertainty, not become a reassuring score.
- **“The model is finished once the diagram is drawn.”** A threat model is a
  versioned decision artifact, not a static picture.

---
name: assessment-sequence-governance
description: "Validates supplied immutable ordered manifests of opaque defensive assessment actions for authority, safeguards, evidence, and separate-operator review. Use when reviewing assessment sequencing without creating, changing, or executing actions."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Assessment sequence governance

## When to Use

- Reviewing assessment sequencing without creating, changing, or executing actions.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Purpose

Validate a supplied ledger without designing the assessment. A passing result
means only that the recorded sequence is internally consistent for separate
review. It is never execution authority.

## Boundary

Never create, select, add, remove, reorder, rank, or substitute actions or
dependencies. Never choose targets, routes, tactics, timing, or tools. Never
schedule or run anything. Do not provide commands, queries, configurations,
credentials, payloads, protocols, infrastructure, stealth, or deployment
guidance. Accept opaque identifiers and digests only.

## Workflow

1. Obtain the already-supplied immutable ledger and confirm the operator wants
   an offline governance review.
2. Stop if the material contains operational instructions or live identifiers.
   Do not quote the rejected value.
3. Preserve the supplied manifest and action order byte-for-byte. Do not repair
   missing actions, dependencies, bindings, or evidence.
4. Reject malformed shapes, types, references, timestamps, digests, restricted
   content, duplicate identifiers, and an empty assessment universe.
5. Keep manifest integrity separate from action identity, authority,
   prerequisites, environment, budget, stop, cleanup, and custody coverage.
6. Require exact action, sequence, manifest, scope, environment, policy,
   authority, and window joins. Similar-looking records never substitute.
7. Preserve supplied predecessor sets. Verify acyclicity, contiguous ordinals,
   and predecessor chronology; do not improve or reorder the sequence.
8. Treat budgets as nontransferable reservations with nonnegative integer
   attempts, duration, impact, and evidence-byte dimensions.
9. Require a passed stop pretest, an armed available stop, and exact action-set
   binding. Bind canonical budget, stop, and cleanup fingerprints through the
   authority and every supporting evidence record.
10. Accept cleanup `not-required` only with exact current policy proof. Never
    infer cleanup from silence.
11. Count every action against all nine required coverage roles. Never omit a
    blocked, prohibited, or historical action.
12. Derive the gate in precedence order: `prohibited`, `approval-required`,
    `blocked`, then `sequence-consistent`.
13. Treat a recorded handoff as historical custody of review work, not
    permission. Derive `withdrawal-required` after authority expiry or
    revocation, manifest or action drift, budget exhaustion, a fired or lost
    stop, cleanup loss, or custody loss.
14. Accept `withdrawn` only from a later exact withdrawal receipt. Never infer
    retry, resumption, or restored authority.

## Report

State the manifest identifier, derived gate, handoff state, contradictions,
coverage gaps, and withdrawal obligations. Add: “Internal consistency only;
separate review is required; no execution authority is granted.”

## Rationalizations to reject

- **“The order is obviously intended.”** Intent cannot repair an immutable
  manifest.
- **“A nearby authorization is close enough.”** Authority is an exact tuple.
- **“Unused budget can move to another action.”** Reservations do not transfer.
- **“The stop can be tested later.”** Readiness requires a passed prior pretest.
- **“No cleanup is probably needed.”** Not-required needs current policy proof.
- **“A recorded handoff permits the run.”** Handoffs grant no authority.
- **“We can reorder one dependency to make it safe.”** This skill never edits
  the supplied sequence.
- **“The record is complete, so proceed.”** Completeness means internally
  consistent for separate review only.

  consistent for separate review only.

# Engagement report assembly

Use this skill to answer one question: does the package faithfully and completely represent the declared engagement universe and every eligible supplied artifact?

## When to Use

- Assemble evidence-backed engagement reports.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Hold the boundary

1. Accept only supplied validated specialist artifacts and administrative receipts.
2. Do not scan, test, reinterpret, rewrite, rescore, merge, split, close, suppress, rank, publish, deliver, notify, sign, or contact.
3. Keep raw evidence, secrets, personal data, payloads, commands, paths, live identifiers, and report prose outside the ledger.

## Declare the universe

1. Record the immutable expected source universe, authority-bound admissions, engagement authority, policy, cutoff, and strict window. Obtain the expected authority-manifest digest independently of the package; never derive or replace it while validating the package.
2. Record supplied scope units, objectives, methods, and limitations without adding or improving them.
3. Give every expected input exactly one disposition: eligible current, eligible historical, boundary-only, excluded invalid, excluded out of scope, or conflicted.

## Preserve source meaning

1. Preserve each external assessment result. Bind its exact capability/version, artifact format, artifact, exit contract, disposition, inclusion, policy, assessment window, manifests, scope, origin, custody, and presentation approval in a separate authority admission; use the registry assembly digest only for packaging.
2. Include every eligible claim and finding exactly once.
3. Preserve claim polarity, state, confidence, applicable status, freshness, and limitations. Never strengthen or reverse them. Represent not-applicable only as a policy-backed coverage cell, never as a claim.
4. Preserve every immutable finding field digest and ordinal. Never retitle, paraphrase, rescore, reorder, merge, split, suppress, or change remediation state.
5. Count shared origin lineage once; duplicate transformations are not corroboration.
6. Keep stale or disposed sources historical. They cannot support current coverage.

## Preserve open truth

1. Keep the full scope-by-objective denominator, including blocked, unknown, gap, prohibited, and not-applicable cells.
2. Bind each cell to exact applicable claims whose scope, objective, polarity, state, confidence, freshness, sources, and evidence derive the cell state. A not-applicable cell has no claims and requires an exact typed current policy receipt whose reason matches the declared scope kind.
3. Represent every independent-origin eligible opposing claim pair with one exact open contradiction; shared-origin transformations never add corroboration.
4. Keep evidence gaps as gaps and findings as findings.
5. Keep implementation and ticket receipts distinct from later remediation verification.
6. Cleanup completion is not evidence disposition, and neither closes a finding.

## Assemble deterministically

1. Include every required appendix exactly once with no dangling or unreferenced member.
2. Recompute every record digest plus section, appendix, manifest, package, and presentation fingerprints from canonical ID-sorted membership.
3. Make rendered presentation membership and order match canonical sections followed by canonical appendices exactly.
4. Recompute factual counts and exact identifier sets. Do not produce a score, grade, maturity, compliance, certification, or all-clear statement.
5. A correction creates version N from one admitted N-1 package receipt with the exact superseded digest; never mutate a released package in place.

## Review package

| Section | Source of truth |
| --- | --- |
| Scope and objectives | Supplied engagement authority and scope records |
| Methods and limitations | Admitted specialist artifacts; preserve their wording and bounds |
| Coverage | Full scope-by-objective denominator, including blocked and unknown cells |
| Findings | Immutable final finding records, included exactly once |
| Contradictions and gaps | Open records; assembly does not resolve or hide them |
| Evidence index | Exact identifiers, custody state, and presentation approval |
| Appendices | Canonical membership and order, with no dangling members |
| Release receipt | Package version, independently supplied authority digest, package digest, and supersession link |

The package is review-ready when every expected input has one disposition and
every eligible artifact is represented. It is not automatically approved,
signed, delivered, or published.

## Rationalizations to reject

- “A nonzero source is invalid.” Claim-bearing nonzero results can be eligible.
- “Rewrite the finding for readability.” Immutable findings remain byte-bound by field digests.
- “Drop unknown or blocked rows.” They remain in the coverage denominator.
- “Resolve the contradiction in prose.” Assembly preserves it for review.
- “The ticket says fixed.” Implementation is not verification.
- “Disposed evidence can still support the current claim.” It is historical only.
- “Add a posture score for executives.” This package has factual counts, never a score.
- “Send the finished report.” This skill never publishes, delivers, signs, or contacts.

skills.name: findings-report
skills.desc: Writes security findings that survive triage: reproducible, severity-justified, and fixable, in a fixed structure with a severity rubric. Use when turning a discovered vulnerability, misconfiguration, or weakness into a report entry, ticket, or disclosure.
skills.body:
---
name: findings-report
description: "Writes security findings that survive triage: reproducible, severity-justified, and fixable, in a fixed structure with a severity rubric. Use when turning a discovered vulnerability, misconfiguration, or weakness into a report entry, ticket, or disclosure."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Writing security findings

A finding is an argument: here is a flaw, here is how to see it yourself,
here is what it costs you, here is what to do. Most findings fail at triage
because one of those four is missing or because the severity was asserted
rather than derived. This skill produces findings in a fixed shape and checks
the argument before prose can hide a missing part.

## When to Use

- Turning a discovered vulnerability, misconfiguration, or weakness into a report entry, ticket, or disclosure.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Quick start

1. Collect, before writing a word: the exact reproduction (input, steps,
   observed result), the affected component and version, and evidence
   (output, screenshot path, request/response). If you cannot reproduce it,
   it is a *lead*, not a finding; label it as such.
2. Fill `references/finding-template.md` from the checked record. Every
   section is required. "N/A" is acceptable only for `References`.
3. Write the fix as a concrete change, not a category. "Validate input" is a
   category. "Reject `path` values that resolve outside `DATA_ROOT` after
   `os.path.realpath`" is a fix.
4. Reread the title. It should name the component and the flaw, and a reader
   should be able to guess the severity from it.

## Finding or lead

| Evidence state | Report as | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reproduced flaw with bounded impact | Finding with severity | The argument can be independently checked |
| Strong signal, reproduction incomplete | Unrated lead | The signal deserves follow-up but impact is not established |
| Version or pattern match only | Observation or lead | Applicability is not proven by a label |
| Control claimed but not verified | Open precondition | A stated control cannot reduce severity without evidence |
| Work blocked by scope or safety limit | Limitation | Blocked work is not a negative result |

Example: a response containing another user's record supports an authorization
finding. A route name containing `admin` does not; it is a lead until access and
impact are demonstrated.

## Rules that keep findings credible

- **One flaw per finding.** Two flaws in one entry get one fix and one
  severity, and one of them is wrong.
- **Reproduce in the reader's environment, not yours.** Replace your paths,
  hostnames and tokens with the reader's or with placeholders they can fill.
- **Quote the evidence, do not describe it.** Paste the response body, the
  log line, the stack trace. Trim, do not paraphrase.
- **Impact is what an attacker gets, not what the bug is.** "SQL injection"
  is the bug. "Read any row in `users`, including password hashes, as an
  unauthenticated caller" is the impact.
- **Quantifiers are evidence claims.** One tested account and two records prove
  that account reached those records. They do not prove every account, every
  record, or exploitation at scale. State the demonstrated set, then label
  broader blast radius as a hypothesis requiring coverage evidence.
- **Likelihood is about preconditions.** Say what the attacker needs:
  network position, an account, a victim click, a race. Each precondition
  lowers likelihood; say so explicitly.
- **Never pad with speculation.** "Could potentially lead to RCE" without a
  demonstrated path is a lead. Put it in `Notes`, not `Impact`.
- **Fix and mitigation are different.** The fix removes the flaw. A
  mitigation reduces exposure while the fix is pending. Label each.

## Severity in one line each

| Severity | Shape of the justification |
| --- | --- |
| Critical | Unauthenticated or low-privilege attacker gets full control or all data, no victim interaction |
| High | Significant data or control, with one precondition (account, victim action, adjacent network) |
| Medium | Limited data or control, or significant impact behind two or more preconditions |
| Low | Information useful for other attacks, or impact confined to the attacker's own session |
| Info | No direct security impact; hygiene, defense in depth, or a deviation from stated policy |

Full rubric with worked examples: `references/severity-rubric.md`.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **"The prose makes the severity obvious."** Readers can disagree; the
  normalized factors and review make the decision reproducible.
- **"The screenshot exists somewhere."** If the record cannot point to it,
  triage cannot verify the claim.
- **"This lead is probably critical."** Unreproduced escalation stays an
  unrated lead until evidence establishes its impact.
- **"The IDs are predictable, so every record is exposed."** Predictability
  supports a follow-up hypothesis; only tested coverage or authoritative access
  logic supports a universal impact claim.
- **"The workaround is good enough to call a fix."** A mitigation reduces
  exposure and states its limit; only a change that removes the flaw is a fix.

skills.name: security-test-tool-governance
skills.desc: Governs supplied benign security-test tool artifacts through purpose, authority, provenance, artifact integrity, safety-test evidence, version-bound review, custody, change control, and defensive handoff. Use when reviewing proposed security tooling or deciding whether an externally supplied artifact is ready for an authorized isolated test, without generating source code, payloads, build procedures, bypasses, or deployment instructions.
skills.body:
---
name: security-test-tool-governance
description: "Governs supplied benign security-test tool artifacts through purpose, authority, provenance, artifact integrity, safety-test evidence, version-bound review, custody, change control, and defensive handoff. Use when reviewing proposed security tooling or deciding whether an externally supplied artifact is ready for an authorized isolated test, without generating source code, payloads, build procedures, bypasses, or deployment instructions."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Security test tool governance

Produce an evidence-bound ledger for externally supplied opaque benign artifacts.

## When to Use

- Reviewing proposed security tooling or deciding whether an externally supplied artifact is ready for an authorized isolated test, without generating source code, payloads, build procedures, bypasses, or deployment instructions.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Boundary

Accept inventory facts and external receipts only. Never fetch, reconstruct,
modify, compile, sign, execute, deploy, or distribute a referenced tool. Never
provide source code, pseudocode, tool commands or flags, build recipes, payloads,
loaders, injection or in-memory execution instructions, persistence, credential
access, lateral movement, C2, covert channels, evasion, packing, obfuscation,
signature avoidance, telemetry blinding, security-control tampering, target
selection or locators, stealth rankings, or quieter-tool recommendations.

Only isolated labs and dedicated non-production test tenants with explicit
separation evidence are supported. Release is an externally evidenced controlled
handoff to an approved internal lab. Production use, customer deployment, public
distribution, and operational use have no contract state. Restricted or unknown
capabilities are inventory facts that force prohibition and quarantine; an
authorization cannot waive that boundary.

## Workflow

1. Record purpose, policy snapshot, assessment cutoff, scope, authority window,
   permitted governance actions, operator roles, non-production boundary, and
   numeric ceilings. Missing authority remains visible; governance readiness
   never grants execution authority.
2. Register each supplied artifact, source, configuration, supplier, component,
   and declared capability using only opaque references and exact SHA-256
   digests. A digest establishes identity, not safety. Do not open opaque content
   to fill an evidence gap.
3. Have the offline review recompute the versioned canonical manifest from
   candidate identity and sorted component/capability declarations. Any material
   change requires a replacement candidate and fresh downstream evidence; a
   supplied digest assertion cannot inherit prior approval.
4. Pin the sandbox fingerprint, synthetic-data boundary, production separation,
   containment, rollback baseline, and validity window. Drift invalidates current
   claims even when the artifact bytes are unchanged.
5. Instantiate all assurance criteria for every candidate before importing
   results. Applicability comes from the artifact-class matrix. Keep planned,
   failed, blocked, prohibited, inconclusive, and evidence-bound not-applicable
   cells in the denominator; absence is never a pass.
6. Import separate provenance, integrity, dependency/source review, independent
   review, containment, functional, safety, observability, stop, and restoration
   receipts. Every supporting member must match its exact binding tuple and
   chronology. Supplier attestations cannot substitute for independent review;
   execution evidence cannot substitute for criterion-outcome evidence.
7. Record current readiness gates, reserved and consumed budgets, applicable
   successfully pretested stop controls, custody readiness, and cleanup readiness.
   Derive readiness from these records, authority, identity, coverage, and issues.
   Preserve approval-required, blocked, and prohibited states without laundering
   them into lab-ready.
8. Import facts from separately authorized bounded synthetic lab validation.
   This workflow does not perform it. Bind each run to its exact case, authority,
   candidate/manifest, sandbox/fingerprint, policy, gate, budget, stop, and cleanup
   records. Keep execution, criterion outcome, observability, stop event, and
   cleanup receipts distinct. Failed and stopped runs consume budget; a fired
   stop is terminal. A retry needs remaining capacity and a later decision.
9. Preserve custody for each evidence artifact and its aliases. Keep failed,
   stopped, inconclusive, and unexecuted cases. Evidence disposal requires its own
   external authority and receipt; endpoint cleanup cannot authorize it. Record
   cleanup separately and retain blocked or failed restoration obligations.
10. Derive issues and remediation from assurance failures and contradictions.
    A supplied change receipt does not close an issue. Record externally
    authorized change, a materially new replacement candidate, and later exact
    verification of the original criterion in an equivalent approved sandbox.
    Preserve the failed candidate, supporting evidence, and unresolved issues.
11. Derive lab eligibility only with complete applicable passing assurance,
    current identities and approval, complete run cleanup, and no blocking or
    prohibited capability. Validate a supplied release occurrence receipt against
    the exact candidate, manifest, artifact, sandbox, scope, policy, authority,
    internal-lab recipient, channel, owner, and window. Have the review recompute
    the canonical handoff digest over the exact recipient and release facts;
    recipient class is only `internal-lab`, and channels are only
    `controlled-repository`, `sealed-offline-media`, or `managed-lab-import`;
    approval, occurrence, and withdrawal receipts must bind that digest. Changed
    handoff facts invalidate inherited receipts. Occurrence is not approval.
12. Derive expiry and withdrawal obligations after authority expiry/revocation,
    policy or sandbox drift, material change, disposed evidence, prohibited
    behavior, or a blocking issue. A later exact withdrawal receipt records
    withdrawn. Export opaque blocker, cleanup, issue, remediation, and handoff
    IDs to defensive owners without operational instructions.

13. Treat a complete review as an internally consistent record only. It never
    establishes authenticity, safety, execution authority, production
    suitability, or release permission.

## Boundary with adjacent skills

`detection-resilience-test-plan` owns separate hypotheses, attempts, defensive
outcomes, test cleanup, and detector remediation. This skill owns artifact
provenance, assurance, custody, version validity, and defensive handoff beforehand.
Neither constructs implementations. `protocol-exploitation-assessment` owns
service weakness applicability and bounded reproduced faults; do not emit protocol
requests or vulnerability proofs here. `opsec-planning` owns observer analysis;
do not select quieter tools. `recon-automation-governance` owns jobs, targets,
schedules, contact budgets, and orchestration; this skill owns candidate assurance.
`findings-report` owns final findings and impact-derived severity. Export typed
assurance issues here, without assigning vulnerability ratings.
`binary-fault-triage` and `binary-fault-validation-readiness` own binary fault
prerequisites; never derive exploit primitives or feasibility here.
`engagement-report-assembly` owns the final engagement report; provide only the
typed governance export.

## Rationalizations to reject

- “The lab is authorized, so generate or execute the helper.” Authority cannot
  waive the opaque-artifact boundary; import external facts instead.
- “It is signed, reproducible, or hash-matched, so it is safe.” These establish
  limited identity/provenance facts and cannot replace independent assurance.
- “The function is optional or disabled.” Restricted or unresolved inventory
  still forces prohibited readiness and quarantined lifecycle.
- “The artifact barely changed; carry forward the review.” Material identity
  includes source, configuration, dependencies, capabilities, sandbox, and policy;
  mismatches invalidate current downstream claims.
- “Discard failed cases or count only tested cells.” This hides the denominator
  and creates unsupported coverage. Preserve every required cell and result.
- “A successful run proves every safety criterion.” Receipt roles and bindings
  are separate; a run cannot satisfy unrelated criteria.
- “Cleanup permits deleting inconvenient evidence.” Custody disposition and
  endpoint restoration need independent authority and receipts.
- “The fix or handoff happened, so approval is implied.” Changes require later
  verification; occurrence receipts never replace approval or withdrawal proof.

   supplied digest assertion cannot inherit prior approval.
4. Pin the sandbox fingerprint, synthetic-data boundary, production separation,
   containment, rollback baseline, and validity window. Drift invalidates current
   claims even when the artifact bytes are unchanged.
5. Instantiate all assurance criteria for every candidate before importing
   results. Applicability comes from the artifact-class matrix. Keep planned,
   failed, blocked, prohibited, inconclusive, and evidence-bound not-applicable
   cells in the denominator; absence is never a pass.
6. Import separate provenance, integrity, dependency/source review, independent
   review, containment, functional, safety, observability, stop, and restoration
   receipts. Every supporting member must match its exact binding tuple and
   chronology. Supplier attestations cannot substitute for independent review;
   execution evidence cannot substitute for criterion-outcome evidence.
7. Record current readiness gates, reserved and consumed budgets, applicable
   successfully pretested stop controls, custody readiness, and cleanup readiness.
   Derive readiness from these records, authority, identity, coverage, and issues.
   Preserve approval-required, blocked, and prohibited states without laundering
   them into lab-ready.
8. Import facts from separately authorized bounded synthetic lab validation.
   This workflow does not perform it. Bind each run to its exact case, authority,
   candidate/manifest, sandbox/fingerprint, policy, gate, budget, stop, and cleanup
   records. Keep execution, criterion outcome, observability, stop event, and
   cleanup receipts distinct. Failed and stopped runs consume budget; a fired
   stop is terminal. A retry needs remaining capacity and a later decision.
9. Preserve custody for each evidence artifact and its aliases. Keep failed,
   stopped, inconclusive, and unexecuted cases. Evidence disposal requires its own
   external authority and receipt; endpoint cleanup cannot authorize it. Record
   cleanup separately and retain blocked or failed restoration obligations.
10. Derive issues and remediation from assurance failures and contradictions.
    A supplied change receipt does not close an issue. Record externally
    authorized change, a materially new replacement candidate, and later exact
    verification of the original criterion in an equivalent approved sandbox.
    Preserve the failed candidate, supporting evidence, and unresolved issues.
11. Derive lab eligibility only with complete applicable passing assurance,
    current identities and approval, complete run cleanup, and no blocking or
    prohibited capability. Validate a supplied release occurrence receipt against
    the exact candidate, manifest, artifact, sandbox, scope, policy, authority,
    internal-lab recipient, channel, owner, and window. Have the review recompute
    the canonical handoff digest over the exact recipient and release facts;
    recipient class is only `internal-lab`, and channels are only
    `controlled-repository`, `sealed-offline-media`, or `managed-lab-import`;

    handoff facts invalidate inherited receipts. Occurrence is not approval.

    policy or sandbox drift, material change, disposed evidence, prohibited
    behavior, or a blocking issue. A later exact withdrawal receipt records
    withdrawn. Export opaque blocker, cleanup, issue, remediation, and handoff
    IDs to defensive owners without operational instructions.

    establishes authenticity, safety, execution authority, production
    suitability, or release permission.

## Boundary with adjacent skills

outcomes, test cleanup, and detector remediation. This skill owns artifact
provenance, assurance, custody, version validity, and defensive handoff beforehand.

requests or vulnerability proofs here. `opsec-planning` owns observer analysis;
do not select quieter tools. `recon-automation-governance` owns jobs, targets,
schedules, contact budgets, and orchestration; this skill owns candidate assurance.

assurance issues here, without assigning vulnerability ratings.

  still forces prohibited readiness and quarantined lifecycle.

  are separate; a run cannot satisfy unrelated criteria.

  endpoint restoration need independent authority and receipts.

  verification; occurrence receipts never replace approval or withdrawal proof.

skills.name: social-engineering-engagement-plan
skills.desc: Plans authorized defensive phishing simulations, vishing exercises, and other social-engineering engagements with explicit channel and cohort scope, pretext approval, participant safety, data minimization, readiness gates, metrics, and debrief. Use before measuring human-security exposure or reviewing a proposed campaign.
skills.body:
---
name: social-engineering-engagement-plan
description: "Plans authorized defensive phishing simulations, vishing exercises, and other social-engineering engagements with explicit channel and cohort scope, pretext approval, participant safety, data minimization, readiness gates, metrics, and debrief. Use before measuring human-security exposure or reviewing a proposed campaign."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Social-engineering engagement plan

Defensive human-security testing measures organizational exposure and validates controls,
but it can cause harm even when every technical action is reversible.
Sponsor authority permits a bounded exercise; it does not prove the target list,
pretext, infrastructure, control cell, support route, or data handling are ready.

This skill creates a checked plan. It does not write deceptive content, call scripts,
payloads, collection pages, target profiles, or execution instructions.

## When to Use

- Plan authorized human-security exercises safely.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Workflow

1. Record the sponsor, window, timezone, owners, digest-bound written-authority
   evidence, its approving role and validity window, allowed and prohibited channels,
   asks, persona classes, themes, and actions. The v0.1 contract supports email and
   voice only; keep every other channel prohibited.
2. Define each target cohort by opaque ID, channel, supplied population, opaque
   inclusion and exclusion references, list state, and evidence. Never store
   addresses, numbers, names, or descriptive dossiers.
3. Describe pretexts by ID, persona class, channel, approved ask, state, evidence,
   and limitations. Store no message copy or scripts.
4. Inventory the target list, sending domain, training page, callback number, control
   cell, and support route as applicable. Planned infrastructure is not verified.
5. Define interaction stops for distress, participant request, reporting, active
   incidents, and out-of-scope people or data. Define campaign pauses for cumulative
   distress, client incidents, scope-risking defects, and loss of the control cell.
   Record whether a pause fired and bind a threshold-triggered pause to evidence.
6. Minimize data before execution. Allow only named event types; use opaque identities,
   aggregate reporting, no individual ranking, no public identification, and an owner
   for retention or disposition. Before readiness, choose no retention or a bounded
   retention period and name the disposition method. An unapproved event is not a
   useful extra metric.
7. Link each planned action to one authorization, cohort, approved pretext, safety
   policy, data policy, and every required infrastructure item. Keep it `planned`
   until all readiness evidence exists.
8. For executed actions, cite chronologically valid event-export or operator-log
   evidence and record bounded aggregate counts. Keep unexecuted and unapproved event
   fields null: zero is an observed measurement, not absence of collection. Never
   infer opens, delivery, reports, distress, or control adherence.
9. Cover authorization, cohort, pretext, infrastructure, safety, data handling,
   deconfliction, debrief, measurement, and reporting for every allowed channel.
10. Record immediate and organization-wide debrief ownership, participant support,
    feedback timing, and no-shaming rules.

## Boundary with adjacent skills

- Use `osint-scanner` or `social-engineering-recon` to collect public intelligence.
- Use `opsec-planning` to compare detection risk and operational artifacts.
- Use this skill to govern authorized interaction with people and participant care.
- Use `findings-report` after evidenced results exist.
- Credential collection, payload delivery, physical-entry methods, and target-system
  access require separate capabilities and explicit authority.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **"The sponsor approved phishing, so the campaign is ready."** Approval does not
  verify the target list, pretext, infrastructure, control cell, or support route.
- **"Open rate is standard."** If open tracking was not approved, it is prohibited
  data collection rather than a free metric.
- **"A click means the participant was compromised."** It proves only the approved
  event that was observed; credentials, execution, and access remain separate.
- **"We can exclude people manually during launch."** Exclusions belong in the
  checked target manifest before contact.
- **"Stopping one call handles distress."** Individual stops and campaign-wide pause
  thresholds solve different safety problems; both are required.
- **"Zero means we did not collect it."** Zero is a measured result. Prohibited or
  uncollected events stay null so the record cannot disguise unauthorized telemetry.
- **"Recording helps evidence."** Recording requires explicit authorization and legal
  review. A useful artifact does not create permission.
- **"Individual rankings make training actionable."** They increase harm and suppress
  reporting. Report cohort and process controls unless individual handling is approved.
- **"A successful test should stay secret until the report."** Timely debrief and a
  private support route are part of the engagement, not optional cleanup.

skills.name: active-directory-attack-path
skills.desc: Analyzes and prioritizes Active Directory and BloodHound attack paths using evidence freshness, disabled principals, prerequisites, authorization, operational noise, and remediation coverage. Use during an authorized red-team operation when reviewing AD graphs, nested groups, ACL abuse, delegation, sessions, GPO control, or routes to Tier Zero.
skills.body:
---
name: active-directory-attack-path
description: "Analyzes and prioritizes Active Directory and BloodHound attack paths using evidence freshness, disabled principals, prerequisites, authorization, operational noise, and remediation coverage. Use during an authorized red-team operation when reviewing AD graphs, nested groups, ACL abuse, delegation, sessions, GPO control, or routes to Tier Zero."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# Active Directory attack paths

A graph relationship describes possible control. It does not prove current
session state, usable credentials, authorized traversal, or the best route for
an operation. Keep those claims separate.

## When to Use

- An authorized red-team operation when reviewing AD graphs, nested groups, ACL abuse, delegation, sessions, GPO control, or routes to Tier Zero.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Workflow

1. Confirm the owned starting principals, high-value objectives, allowed
   evidence reads, allowed traversal actions, and acceptable operational noise.
2. Inventory relevant users, groups, computers, GPOs, domains, and trusts.
   Record whether user and computer accounts are enabled and when volatile
   evidence was collected.
3. Normalize group membership, administrative rights, object-control rights,
   delegation, GPO-derived control, trusts, and session observations as directed
   edges. Resolve nested membership before declaring an effective path.
4. Give every node and edge an evidence reference and disposition. Current LDAP
   or security-descriptor evidence can establish a configuration relationship;
   stale session evidence remains a candidate.
5. Enumerate materially distinct paths from each owned principal to each stated
   objective. Include blocked branches when they explain why a visually
   connected graph is not viable.
6. For every edge, record required actions and operational noise. A structurally
   proven path may still require separate approval for a password reset, host
   access, credential interaction, authentication, ticket request, or state
   change.
7. Add remediations that sever every objective path. Prefer the smallest set of
   relationships or principals that removes the largest amount of reachability.
8. Report graph confidence and execution disposition separately. State that
    coverage applies to the supplied graph, not necessarily the whole domain.

## Path decision table

| Evidence state | Path disposition |
| --- | --- |
| Current configuration evidence, met prerequisites, and every action authorized | Validation candidate; still not achieved access until executed |
| Current configuration evidence but an active transition lacks approval | Structurally proven, approval required |
| Stale session or unverified credential availability | Plausible candidate, not a current path |
| Disabled principal, unmet prerequisite, explicit deny, or prohibited action | Blocked at the named edge |
| Missing graph segment or unknown evidence freshness | Unknown; preserve the gap |

For each objective, report materially distinct paths, the weakest edge in each,
required actions, operational signal, authorization state, and the smallest
remediation set that severs all reported routes.

## Interpretation rules

- A disabled user can retain group membership while blocking a current
  authentication path. Preserve both facts.
- `HasSession` is volatile. Its age, logon type, and credential availability
  determine whether it is evidence or only a lead.
- Object control establishes authority over the object. It does not establish
  that changing the object is authorized or operationally quiet.
- Membership, GPO application, credential access, authentication, and downstream
  impact are separate transitions.
- An edge after the objective may show business impact without belonging to the
  path used to reach that objective.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **"BloodHound drew a line, so the path works."** Graph data can be stale,
  incomplete, or dependent on disabled principals and unmet prerequisites.
- **"The shortest path is the best path."** A short password reset can be more
  disruptive and detectable than a longer read-only validation route.
- **"Membership proves authentication."** Disabled accounts and missing
  credential material can make a valid membership edge operationally useless.
- **"AdminTo proves credentials are available."** Host control and a session
  observation are separate claims; session material may be absent or protected.
- **"Read-only authorization covers harmless validation."** Resets, logons,
  ticket requests, host access, credential interaction, and policy changes are
  active actions regardless of intent.
- **"Fixing the first edge closes the domain."** Every distinct objective path
  needs an explicit severing control and evidence after remediation.

skills.name: adcs-exposure-audit
skills.desc: Audits Active Directory Certificate Services configuration for dangerous certificate templates, PKI ACLs, enrollment interfaces, mapping policy, and identity escalation paths. Use during an authorized identity security review when assessing AD CS, certificate templates, enterprise CAs, or Certipy-style inventory without exercising an attack path.
skills.body:
---
name: adcs-exposure-audit
description: "Audits Active Directory Certificate Services configuration for dangerous certificate templates, PKI ACLs, enrollment interfaces, mapping policy, and identity escalation paths. Use during an authorized identity security review when assessing AD CS, certificate templates, enterprise CAs, or Certipy-style inventory without exercising an attack path."
allowed-tools: Read Grep Glob
---

# AD CS exposure audit

AD CS issues are combinations. A broad enrollment ACL alone may be intended;
the same ACL combined with an authentication purpose, requester-controlled
identity, and weak issuance controls becomes an escalation surface. Record
facts separately and derive the combinations.

## When to Use

- An authorized identity security review when assessing AD CS, certificate templates, enterprise CAs, or Certipy-style inventory without exercising an attack path.
- Use only within explicit authorization and the stated rules of engagement.

## When NOT to Use

- Do not treat this skill as permission to access, test, or change a target.
- Do not convert missing evidence into a clean result or a stronger claim.

## Workflow

1. Confirm the authorized domains, CAs, directory objects, and read-only
   collection actions. Do not request a certificate, relay authentication,
   coerce authentication, modify an object, or attempt certificate logon
   unless those actions are separately authorized.
2. Inventory every enterprise CA and every template it publishes. Record CA
   flags, SID-extension policy, patch state, enrollment interfaces,
   administrative rights, HSM signing controls, and enrollment-agent
   restrictions.
3. Record template publication, schema version, effective enrollment
   principals, subject-supply behavior, EKUs or application policies,
   approval, authorized signatures, SID-extension behavior, and issuance
   policy OIDs. For templates requiring authorized signatures, record the
   required registration-authority application policies.
4. Record effective ACLs on templates, CA configuration, NTAuthCertificates,
   enrollment services, CA computer objects, and OID objects. Resolve nested
   membership before calling a principal low privilege.
5. Record certificate mapping on every relevant domain controller and
   certificate-authenticating service. Include strong binding mode, enabled
   Schannel mapping methods, and explicit `altSecurityIdentities` mappings.

## Interpretation rules

- Treat template, CA, network, mapping, and directory-control findings as
  separate claims even when they form one path.
- Strong KDC mapping can block a specific arbitrary-identity path while the
  source template remains dangerously broad for other certificate consumers.
- HTTPS alone does not resolve NTLM relay exposure. Record Extended Protection
  and channel-binding enforcement.
- A missing SID extension is a configuration exposure. Its exploitation path
  still depends on mapping policy or another identity-injection condition.
- `ManageCA`, certificate-manager rights, template control, and PKI-object
  control are not interchangeable; report the authority actually observed.
- Absence from the supplied inventory is unknown, not clean.

## Rationalizations to reject

- **"Certipy did not label it vulnerable."** Tool labels cannot replace the
  underlying template, ACL, CA, mapping, and endpoint facts.
- **"Full enforcement makes subject supply harmless."** It constrains KDC
  mapping; other certificate consumers and chained configuration changes
  remain in scope.
- **"The right is expected, so it is safe."** Expected Tier Zero authority
  still needs an accountable owner and evidence. Low-privilege authority is
  an exposure regardless of intent.
- **"We can prove it by requesting one certificate."** A configuration audit
  does not create credentials or exercise identity paths without separate
  authorization.
- **"ESC numbering is the finding."** Describe the actual control failure and
  conditions; catalogs evolve.
